National Design Council

Mr. Speaker, in December, 1960, responsibility for the national industrial design council was transferred from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. For a number of years the council had functioned as a committee of the national gallery of Canada. Its prime responsibility was to foster greater appreciation and use of good industrial design in Canada. In addition the council worked closely with the design centre in Ottawa where exhibits of good design were on public display. Also, the council sponsored a number of travelling exhibitions of good design.
In recent years the council and design centre were increasingly active in the field of industrial and commercial design. It was thought, therefore, that this work could more appropriately be carried out in closer liaison with the Department of Trade and Commerce. For the reasons it was deemed advisable to transfer the council to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to make the staff of the gallery, assigned to this work, a part of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The government places great importance on the development of good design as one means of helping to make Canadian goods competitive with those of other countries. It is not always realized that design as well as price is an important factor in market competitiveness. Good design incorporates two basic features, style and function. A commodity must be designed in such a way that it can be readily used to its full potential.
With respect to industrial goods this is an important cost factor. Industrial goods should be designed so they can be used most efficiently while in operation. At the same time they must incorporate such features as safety, adaptability and ease of servicing. In any industrial enterprise these are important cost considerations. The functional qualities of commodities are also important factors in the sale of consumer goods. Appliances, household utensils, clothing, recreational goods and the great range of consumer items should each be designed to best fulfil their intended functions if they are to receive consumer approval.
In designing a product, however, style is also important. If a commodity is to sell it should be pleasing. It must have an attractive and decorative form which complements its functional qualities. Both industry and the general public are becoming more conscious of good design and are demanding that good design be incorporated in the goods they purchase. It must be emphasized that, with the present state of competition in markets both at home and abroad, Canadian industry cannot afford to ignore design as a basic

competitive factor. Canada's competitors are fully aware of this importance. They are continually devoting time and resources to the development and improvement of commodity design which will give them competitive advantages.
If Canadian products are to be able to compete effectively with those of other countries they must also incorporate the best in design as well as compare favourably in both quality and price. Basic design thinking, from the choice of raw materials to the method of production, the actual product design, and the manner of packaging can result in a better product in terms of cost to the producer and in terms of function and appearance to the purchaser. This is an enormous field of endeavour, and full co-operation among manufacturers, distributors, consumers and government is needed if we are to achieve the desired results.
In order to better assist Canadian industry in achieving these objectives it has been decided by the government to introduce legislation to place the national design council on a more permanent basis, and to give it a recognized official status. The council is to consist of 17 members chosen from the fields of industry and commerce, distribution, architecture, design and engineering, and from departments of government which have a specialized interest in design. In addition there is provision for representation from the general public on the council. Members will be appointed by the governor in council to serve for three-year terms.
The objects of the council are to promote and expedite improvement of design in the products of Canadian industry. The council will plan and implement programs to create an awareness by industry and the general public of the need for good design. It will develop methods of achieving improved design, assist industry in developing and applying good design techniques, and organize and assist committees to implement programs to foster good design. It will encourage study and research in design and will be able to recommend the granting of scholarships and grants for such purposes. For a number of years the council has sponsored the granting of awards of merit to Canadian products of outstanding design. This work will be continued and expanded.
It is the government's intention that in the future the council will work in closer cooperation with Canadian designers, manufacturers, distributors and representatives of the general public. While the main responsibility for developing good designs must rest with Canadian industry, we believe that the council and the Department of Trade and Commerce can give valuable assistance to

industry in achieving these goals. I might mention that government sponsored design councils and agencies in the United Kingdom and Europe, particularly in the Scandinavian countries, have been active tor a considerable time and have achieved notable successes. We are very hopeful that the newly constituted council will continue the good work of its predecessor, and that as a result of this legislation it will be in a position to be an even more effective instrument of making Canadian design second to none.

Mr. Speaker, we live in a country where we trade not only because we have commodities to trade but also because we have commodities which we must trade. Canada is a trading country, and as such nobody would deny the importance of good design in those commodities which we have to sell. Good design in those commodities is not only important in selling them within the confines of our own country; good design is also important if our commodities are to be sold in the markets of the world. Our commodities, to be sold in Canada and in the markets of the world, must not only be attractive as far as price is concerned but must also be attractive as far as design is concerned.
I think every effort should be made to arrive at some basic design which can be recognized as a Canadian design and not merely a variation in style based on the design of some other country. I think there is a distinct difference between style and basic design. If our commodities are going to be attractive to people in other countries our basic design should be such as to be recognized as distinctively Canadian. Our design should be such as to meet the modern demands which are made of design.
I think, for example, of good Canadian design in household and office furniture, household appliances, children's toys, electronic equipment; and particularly I think of good design in commodities which are going to be sold to tourists who visit our country during the warmer part of the year. I believe there is something fundamentally wrong in selling to tourists commodities that are produced in their own country.
Not only do we want to develop commodities for the tourist trade that are national in design, but we should develop commodities which are regional in design for sale to tourists. I would hope that in the not too distant future serious consideration might be given to the commodities that form an important part of our tourist trade, to the end that they would be designed not only nationally but on a regional basis. If a commodity were designed nationally it should be
National Design Council designed in such a way to be recognized as Canadian, and if designed for regional purposes it should be designed in such a way as to be recognized as coming from a particular region of Canada.
Another field to which we should give serious consideration is that of packaging. We have a great many commodities in this country which we want to sell particularly in our groceterias and large chain stores. Packaging, here, is particularly important. I believe that a good deal of work can be done in order to ensure that the designs produced for packaged foodstuffs and other articles are such as to attract the people who would wish to buy them.
I entirely agree with the purpose of this bill. I believe it is a good move to have the national design council removed from the national gallery to the Department of Trade and Commerce at a time when we are particularly aware of the need for increasing our sales abroad. However, I should point out that this bill is not going to give the government authority to do any more than it now has authority to do.
The industrial design committee was formed in June of 1948. This committee was charged with the responsibility of ensuring that Canadian talent was used to the fullest possible extent in developing good Canadian design. If we examine the bill now before us we can see very clearly that it provides nothing new. While all of us here would be in accord with the principle of the bill, it requires to be pointed out that this is a field in which the government already is authorized to act.
In 1953 the original committee changed its name to the national industrial design council. Its purpose was to promote a greater use of Canadian talent in designing all types of consumer goods. At that time there were 30 members appointed to this committee drawn from the fields of manufacturing, retailing, industry, design, research, education and government. A further purpose of the committee was to do everything possible to provide complete information on contemporary design. It also decided that it should award scholarships to students attending university both in our own country and abroad.
One of the main purposes of this committee in the beginning was to study the economic relationship between good design and stability in the industries concerned. Over the years this committee has made a considerable contribution to the design of Canadian commodities. I do not think, however, Canada over the years has been able to attain a particularly important place in world design. I believe that with the raw materials and the

National Design Council industries we have, and with a great deal of attention being paid to good Canadian design by this council, an important contribution could be made. I wish to point out again, however, that while all of us would agree with the purpose of this bill, it does not provide to the present government authority to do those things for which it does not already have authority.
Finally, I wish to reiterate that I believe that in the commodities we have to sell in this country and abroad, a design should be achieved which could be recognized as distinctively Canadian. With a distinctively Canadian design, with prices that are competitive and with materials that are recognized as being of good quality, I believe we shall be able to sell our commodities in increased quantities to other countries of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I believe all hon. members will agree that the principle of this bill is good. The transfer of the design council to the Department of Trade and Commerce, where we feel it rightly belongs, should prove of benefit. This bill is important if only because of the fact that the minister states that more effort will be devoted to the functions of the design council.
It is most unfortunate that Canada definitely has been lagging behind in the field of design as compared with other countries of the world. Irrespective of where the responsibility lies, it cannot be ignored that in sales abroad Canada has been resting on its oars. We have been guilty of thinking that we would continue to enjoy a seller's market as we have in past years. We did not anticipate finding ourselves in our present position in a buyer's market.
If Canada is to increase sales at home, considerable research must be undertaken in designing goods for home consumption that will meet the requirements of Canadian buyers. We are not facing up to facts when we state that a buy Canadian program is not having the hoped for result if no effort is being made to improve the design of commodities for domestic consumption to favourably compete with imported products.
While it is important that design research be undertaken with respect to products for domestic consumption, it is also essential that great attention be paid to design in terms of export trade. I think we should note that what might appeal to the purchaser at home does not of necessity appeal to the purchaser abroad. In the extended work of the design council I sincerely hope that every possible effort will be made to convince the manufacturing industry in Canada that they must have an understanding of the thinking

and the requirements of the people abroad to whom we wish to sell our goods. I know that on many occasions in the past in countries outside Canada I have found that people will say they like our product and inquire why it is not designed to meet their requirements. As I say, Canada has been resting on her oars. Canadian industry has been lagging behind and not recognizing the fact that we just cannot sit back and wait for orders to come in.
I also want to say that I think it is most opportune that on this very matter of design there was a most interesting program on television last week. I think we should take not of that broadcast and of what was said, because the people who were interviewed had some interest in design. They included, shall I say, captains of industry, research men and the head of the national research council.
What did we hear from all those men? We heard that Canada is not doing the job it should do on research and on design. The opinion was almost unanimous that Canada is far behind other countries, particularly the United States and the Scandinavian countries, in this matter of design. It was pointed out that only a few countries are paying much attention to research and design.
I do not know how it is going to be done, but I feel that this council has a big task ahead of it in trying to drive home to industry the fact that this is a subject with regard to which they cannot rely on the design council nor upon the national research council, but that they have a most serious responsibility which they themselves must accept. The council is going to be obliged to exert every possible bit of influence and pressure on industry, which unfortunately in the past has wanted to sit back and hope that its profits will continue. Also when there is something new in the way of design, the manufacturers of Canada, if possible, must expand their facilities and produce those goods themselves.
I think the people of Canada who viewed that C.B.C. program last week must have been positively shocked and taken aback at what I would term the betrayal of Canada as a country and of the Canadian people as workers, when the complete evidence was given of new designing done by Canadian research workers and of the fact that nobody wanted to take advantage of it or of the new product and put it into production, with the result that in the one instance the licence was sold to a firm in the United States. That was an instance of Canadian designing but no Canadian production. We are now importing from the United States a product which was designed in Canada and which Canada, as

a manufacturing country, refused to produce. In another instance something new was designed in Canada but Canada would not touch it. Now the licence is in the United Kingdom, and we are going to import the product into Canada.
I have just used these instances in order to point out the great task which lies ahead of this continuing design council under the Department of Trade and Commerce. To use a slang term, we must pull up our socks, we must not lag behind; if it is possible we must establish leadership. All I can say is that I hope the design council can get this message of research and design across to Canadian industry so that we can not only maintain but may expand the purchase of goods which are made in Canada by Canadians and meet the competition from abroad, where research is going on at such a rapid pace.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill. First I should like to commend the minister on the idea set forth. However, the bill only sets up the council. As we all know, the success of the council will depend entirely upon its personnel, and in a minute or so I want to say something about that matter.
Both in their own minds and in the minds of people in a good many other countries there is the idea that Canadians are the producers and manufacturers of the utilitarian. This is one of the drawbacks that we in Canada are obliged to face. I am hopeful that the design council will start in a new direction from that traditional understanding of the Canadian product. We know of products of many types that have gone off the market in recent years for the sole reason that they have not competed in design, in appeal or in ideas with products imported from other countries. Many disappear from the market through lack of imagination on the part of manufacturers who in the past have found a ready market for their products and have been satisfied just to go on so long as the product was sold.
If there is anything that Canada needs in its export trade I believe it is a flair for design, for something different, which will bring it at least up to and possibly beyond the standards of other countries. I am thinking particularly of furniture, silverware, toys and novelties, all of which we are fully capable of manufacturing in Canada but which have fallen behind the products of many other countries in the matter of design, appeal and something new.
I think this is one of the problems which the design council will be obliged to face. As I said, I believe that the personnel of this
National Design Council council will be its most important feature. I hope the council will not be overloaded with members of the stolid, traditional types. I hope we shall not find too many of the personnel listed on it, from the government service and from the traditional manufacturers to the point where any bright ideas that might come up for consideration will be sat upon. I should like to see three or four crackpots put on this council.
Who is available?

Perhaps the general public would put them into that classification, but I refer to people capable of doing advanced thinking, even ahead of our time, on matters of design and artistic practicability. I do not think the minister needs to designate which of the individuals he appoints would come in this category. However, I hope there will be on the design council persons with advanced artistic knowledge so they will bring up the standard of the council to a point where they will accept and promote new and novel ideas in the design of Canadian products.
I think it would be very depressing and an absolute waste of time if we were merely going to pass a bill and put on the council persons who will not advance the ideas which are really behind the bill. Therefore I say to the minister, do not be too traditional in the members who are selected for this council; let us see something of an advance in the traditional Canadian type of utilitarian product which has been manufactured.
I should like to make one further comment, and this concerns the remarks made by the hon. member who preceded me. The hon. member mentioned two cases in which Canadians had manufactured or designed products which could not be produced in Canada. Within my riding there is an example of the other side of the coin, where the minister's department has assisted very much in the production of a Canadian product. For almost a year I have been making efforts on behalf of a man who has designed the most advanced type of printing press in the world today. This is known as the Stroud press. It has attracted the attention of manufacturers in Germany, Sweden and the United States, all of whom have sent persons to look at this particular press. It has also been examined by the national research council and the Queen's printer's office, and has been found to be advanced in its design to the point where it is revolutionary.
The inventor of this press is a patriot who wishes this press to be manufactured in Canada. He has encountered great difficulties. It would be very easy for him to merely

National Design Council sell his patent, as other persons have done, and let the product be manufactured outside this country. However, he has fought for some months now, with the assistance of the minister's department, and it appears that this press is going to be manufactured in Canada with assistance from the Department of Trade and Commerce, the industrial development bank and perhaps with accommodation rented from the Department of Defence Production.
If this develops to the point we hope it will, this will be an excellent example of the manufacture in Canada of a product of new design for export. I wanted to mention this one example in order to illustrate that it is possible, with the assistance of this department, to manufacture products of new design in this country. This can be done, and objects of new design can be accepted, promoted and manufactured in Canada and exported from this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in connection with this bill because of the relationship it may have to the existing and proposed legislation for the protection of industrial designs. As the house knows, we have an old design act in Canada. This act was passed in 1906, and seeks to give a designer some protection for the shape, appearance or configuration of an article of manufacture. This particular act has been very unsatisfactory.
In 1958 we received a report from the royal commission on patents, copyrights, trademarks and industrial designs relating particularly to industrial designs which could be covered by this legislation. The bill, of course, gives no definition1-I do not know whether it is necessary-of what is a design. However, it is interesting to note that there are many kinds of designs; there are mechanical designs, artistic designs and designs relating to the shape, appearance or configuration of an article of manufacture.
I suppose this bill would not cover what could be called an artistic design in the sense of something which really belongs to the arts, but rather would have to do with commercial and industrial designs. The latter is exactly what the old industrial design act covered and protected, and this subject matter will be covered also if the house passes another bill in the future as a result of the report made by the royal commission.
My request to the minister is to find out whether this bill will be related to the industrial design act in such away that if the government assists or suggests designs for industry through this council, it will seek to give protection to the council, to the person who designed it, and to industry, or whether the design will be made available to the


country free of any charge or royalty. As the minister knows, we have gone pretty far in patents, for example. We know that the research council has a very large patent department. Although research is carried out at the expense of the people of Canada, the council obtains patents and royalties are charged to the public who use the patents.
I certainly would not like this idea to creep into this new act, by regulation or otherwise. On the other hand, the line must be drawn as to whether an individual who has invented, if you wish to use that word, or perfected a design and has received some assistance from the council, shall be barred from protection, as against a person who has not sought any assistance at all. Perhaps the minister understands my point. I hope he does. There is that line where an individual creating a new design for industry receives protection now, and will receive more protection under the new act than he has received in the past; whereas I hope a design created exclusively by the council, or entirely with their assistance, will be made available to the public freely, without charge. There is also the case of the poor individual who creates a design in part and receives only some assistance from the council; there is a point as to whether he should receive any protection at all.
This is the only matter I wish to take up at this time, because I do not see anything objectionable in this bill. On the contrary, I think we all agree that we need new designs and shapes for articles of all types manufactured in Canada. However, I think the regulations should be more specific on the question of protection. They could perhaps also be more specific with regard to the definition of a design. There is no definition of a design in this bill, and it might be well to think about this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to approve the principle of this bill. I feel that if this council works in conjunction with industry and our research departments here in Ottawa it could have a very beneficial effect on industry in general in this country. However, I do not like to see Canada sold short, as it were, because I feel that we in this country are quite advanced in many designs both in industry and in different types of manufacturing.
Look at our tourist industry, for example. We have a wide variety of articles which tourists pick up while in Canada, but I hear many tourists complain very bitterly that one can hardly buy any kind of Canadian designed souvenir that is made in Canada. Foreign countries copy our totem poles, our Maid of the Mist plates and design, our mounted police, our Quebec figurettes and our

Eskimo carvings. All these things are definitely of Canadian design, but unfortunately there does not seem to be anything to prevent other countries copying them. Therefore I think in the setting up of this council we must not only consider the question of helping to create new designs for commodities of one kind and another, but also protecting them after they have been designed.
I hope the minister will give that point some consideration, because I think it is very important. I do not think I have anything else to say at this time. Much could be said about this matter. I do feel it is not only a question of designing; it is also a matter of protecting the design after it has been made. Again I must say I disagree with some hon. members when they say that Canada is lagging in design. I do not say we are leading, but in my opinion we are certainly not lagging.

wish to add a few remarks to those already made with reference to this proposed new council. I congratulate the minister on taking the responsibility of accepting an idea proposed and first instituted by the prior administration and in this way complimenting the minister who was at that time responsible.
The party to which I belong has long been interested in design and in the promotion of Canadian manufactured goods which by their design and by their functionality will be able to compete here at home and abroad. No one, I suppose, on this side of the house or on the other side would suggest that better and more suitable design could at any time be a bad thing. However, in the set up of the national design council in Bill No. C-85 which is now before us it may be noted that there is very little dependence on the type of person who might be expected to be called upon, who would be interested by way of his profession. It is noted that only four members will be chosen from the fields of architecture, design and engineering out of a total of 17.
It might be suggested that since design is the whole purpose of the bill there are many in these fields within the dominion who should be called upon, who have formed professional organizations and who should find a place on this council. There is, in fact, a professional association in Canada which is known as the association of Canadian industrial designers, and one would expect that members of that association might be found in the make-up of the proposed council.
There was one reference to a conceivable drawback that was made by the hon. member for Ottawa East and referred to very briefly, I think, by the hon. member for Lincoln, who spoke earlier. In Canada we have had for some years a design council which has been
National Design Council under the aegis of the national gallery. We have had very little advance in new design, and I do wish to make a submission to the minister who will be responsible for this council that perhaps one of the things which will be necessary is the reform of our laws with respect to patents and copyrights and in particular to the registration of new designs.
The Ilsley commission has already been referred to. It was set up by the prior administration, and reported in 1958. There is a report to which I would refer the minister which is available in the library of parliament. It recommends that there should be protection of industrial design, and it may well be that one of the factors inhibiting Canadian designers is that they are not able effectively to obtain the fruit of their labour by registering their designs. In the report of the Ilsley commission there is consideration of recent legislation in the United Kingdom which tightens this matter and a consideration of the pros and cons of extending such provisions.
The Ilsley commission was not able to come to a firm conclusion as to whether giving protection to those who caused new industrial designs to come into being was something which solidified design or whether it was some thing which caused more activity in the design field. But these learned gentlemen, after hearing briefs from a number of interested persons, including a brief from the national design council through its representatives, found themselves in favour of protection and recommended to the government of the day, which is the minister's government, that a new act be drawn which would give to those who created new designs a degree of protection.
I would refer the minister particularly to page 11 of that report of the royal commission on patents, copyrights, trademarks and industrial design, published in 1958 by the Queen's printer. On page 11 appears the report of the Snow committee, which was a committee set up in England to consider this question. The report is properly called the report of the departmental committee appointed by the president of the board of trade of the United Kingdom to consider the patents and designs act. This report goes into some detail regarding the benefit to increasingly good design to be obtained by protecting the holder of the design.
There are, it is true, a number of problems to be considered. There is in existence now the registration act, which is considered to be ineffective and which has been found by those who have perfected new designs not to give them adequate protection. I suggest, therefore, that attention be given not only by

National Design Council the minister but by his colleague the Secretary of State to the revision of those statutes in order that new designs as they are promoted, encouraged and brought into being in Canada shall be assisted, so that one who does a great deal of work and expends a great deal of time in causing these designs to come into being shall be able to obtain, at least for a limited period, protection of that work and talent.
I also suggest to the minister who will be responsible for the new design council that relatively little has been done in Canada to assist or protect or encourage industrial designers. It is known there has been a series of scholarships given in the past, but these scholarships do not appear to have been sufficient in number or large enough in scope to permit the winners to study abroad and then spend considerable time developing new designs here. I know that in the annual report of the national gallery of Canada for 1959-1960, under "Industrial Design", the national industrial design council, which has been set up by the trustees of the national gallery and which I presume will go out of existence on the passage of this bill, has instituted a new series of design awards and a new design index listing Canadian manufactured products which meet certain design specifications, in respect of which certificates are to be given on a three-year basis. It appears in the report that the first year for such awards to be made is 1961, in the autumn, when an international jury is to be set up to choose the winner.
I hope that in causing the national industrial design council to go out of existence at this time, and having it replaced by the national design council, the plans which have been formulated by the earlier council will be continued and developed by the new body. The old body, which I presume, will now go out of existence, was an active executive group of about 12 members who met every three months. In view of the fact that it appears to be unanimous in this house that we should concentrate on the design of Canadian products, and in view of the fact that the minister indicated there should be more energy and attention paid to this particular aspect of design, I suggest that the council should meet far more frequently than is suggested in the proposed act.
The problems which the council will meet in respect of the dissemination of information, and creating public interest in design, are briefly dealt with in section 10 and other sections of the bill, where there is indication that there will be scholarships, publications and travelling shows of the kind that presently exist. I suggest to the minister that there is
[Miss LaMarsh.}

very little new thought here as to the proposed method of operation of this council. There are excellent displays and publications now being made available, one of which was the new booklet put out this year entitled "Design Bulletin" issued as a monthly News Letter, However, I suggest that these are insufficient and that it will be necessary to find other ways of promoting good design.
I think hon. members have seen the display of good design in respect of Christmas gifts which has appeared in Ottawa for the past two or three years under the aegis of the design centre, as well as the travelling exhibitions. I first saw this display when I was in Ottawa as a tourist. Hon. members should realize that these exhibits come to the attention not only of those who live in the area in which they are displayed but, if the area has a large tourist public, a profound impression is made on a great many additional people.
I think it is necessary to educate people in the matter of taste, appreciation and style. This is, of course, a long process. There are a number of magazines, unfortunately most of them United States publications, with perhaps the exception of one which is Canadian, which promote style in the home by photographs and discussions of new styles and new functions in respect of articles used in and around the home as well as building materials. These magazines include photographs of furniture, appliances, gardening tools and many articles of that type. They have been very instrumental in changing the taste of people in this country.
Unfortunately in Canada, whether imported or locally designed and sold, style often is accompanied by high price. It too often appears that the Canadian manufacturer feels, in respect of low priced or minimum priced goods, that design, style or function does not matter and that only those individuals with a good deal of money to spend will be interested. I suggest that it should be a function of this council to persuade manufacturers that this matter of taste is not limited to those potential purchasers with much money to spend but that it is an intrinsic thing, because everyone appreciates beauty and style regardless of their ability or inability to afford them. I suggest that those individuals who are only able to afford a bare minimum would prefer to purchase an article which is both beautiful and functional within their price range.
Those of us on this side could not fail to approve of a concentrated effort on the part of the government and interested people in the community to improve the style of products, making those products not only more saleable but providing a distinct benefit in the

way of beauty to those who purchase them. We could not disapprove of this because legislation of this type was introduced by the party which now sits on your left, Mr. Speaker.
This being 1961, we could hope that those individuals on the newly instituted design council will be looking not just to this year, but ahead to 1981 in doing all there is in their power to bring new designs to our products as quickly as possible, so that design will not be a matter only of beauty to promote sales in Canada but also that we may take pride in Canadian produced articles being sold in shops all around the world. I hope this will take place as quickly as possible so that one can say with pride, that an article is indeed Canadian both in substance and design.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the well designed member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh).
Hear, hear.

There is one thought that I would like to leave with the minister in respect of this bill before us, which follows suggestions made by other members in regard to one of the beneficial effects which will flow from the activities of the design council. I refer, of course, to the potential increase in the sale of Canadian made goods in other countries. There is a group of people in Canada, the largest single organized group of citizens, who are not disinterested in this question of increasing the sales of our commodities in other countries. I suggest that this group has done some research work in the field of design in respect of commodities, goods and packages which would be a marked contribution toward the activities of the design council. Incidentally, this group is represented on the national productivity council, and I feel should be represented on the design council. I refer specifically to the organized labour group in Canada.
It was the promise of this government, although it has not always been carried out, that organized labour would be represented on all the boards, commissions and agencies in which this group is interested. I suggest that this group is interested in the question of design and the promotion of unique designs reflecting Canadian attitude and spirit. This group would be interested in design itself as well as the beneficial effects improved design will have upon the sale of our goods in other countries.
In view of what I have said, I wonder whether the minister would indicate whether this suggestion, in respect of organized labour representation on the design council, is one

National Design Council he considers should be followed. I repeat that I feel this largest single organized group in Canada should be represented so their views and ideas can be reflected as much as possible in the recommendations and activities that may be undertaken by this council.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to support the bill. I think the time is long overdue when we should pay more attention to promoting the skill of our own people and the sale of Canadian goods. In my opinion there is nothing more conducive to such a forward step than a council of this sort. I should like to see a very large contribution made toward scholarships and also by way of grants for exhibitions at local fairs. There is a good deal of talent throughout Canada that never comes to light. There is no point in spending money or having such a council unless we bring this talent to light. We look to our young people for new and better designs. A country that has encouraged such men as Graham Bell does not need to take a back seat in the development not only of new designs but also new instruments.
I am also pleased to see that the bill contemplates the giving of awards of merit. I do not know why such awards should not be retroactive. If there are Canadian designers who have already made contributions I think they should be encouraged. Such awards may encourage them to remain in Canada where their services are needed, particularly if it is in monetary form.
I think it is a forward step that we are going to encourage exhibitions abroad. The reports I have heard about the Brussels fair indicate that Canada's activities there left much to be desired. A good many Canadians went to that fair expecting to be very proud of the Canadian displays but came home disappointed. They were particularly disappointed with the food served. I do not know why Canadian cooking should not be included within the wide scope of this bill. When we go abroad and have European or British guests we should be able to take them to the Canadian pavilion at such fairs and be able to have Alberta steaks, British Columbia salmon or other items produced in Canada which are among the world's finest foods. If we are going to sell abroad we have to display our best products. How can we do it any better than by having Canadian travellers introduce these people to the foods we know so well?
I think our Canadian embassies and consulates should be encouraged to show Canadian goods. I understand that the embassies and consulates of Canada throughout the

National Design Council world are filled with French antique furniture, American colonial furniture or English period furniture. When new consulates are opened I should like to see them equipped with Quebec furniture, Ontario furniture or any other furniture made in Canada so that we can show the people of other lands what we produce. No other country would be foolish enough to advertise other than its own products abroad. I think we have to act like adults now that our country has reached maturity, and fill our embassies and consulates with Canadian made goods. We have beautiful products of all kinds in every industry, and I believe we should promote their sale.
We can learn something from the way other countries do business. Before the Japanese design goods for use in Canada or the United States they send a trade mission here and conduct a kind of Gallup poll. Through our commercial outlets they find out what we want; then they go back to Japan and do not lose any time producing it. We could do the same thing. Perhaps our embassies and consulates do not have the time to do this work, but we could send teams of experts to other countries to find out what they like and then we could produce what these countries want.
I can see a tremendous field so far as forestry is concerned. The people of Asia are now awakening, and they want to be educated. I do not think one could exaggerate the amount of paper products they are going to need. We have the mills and the ability to produce such products. We could send a trade team to Asia to find out what kind of printed products they want, particularly in the form of school books. The people of China, Japan and India are tremendous readers, and here is a field that in my opinion we have not even scratched.
We rely very largely on the forest industry to balance our trade. If we can get those who produce paper and the printers to co-operate, there is no reason why we cannot print material in the languages of the people of these countries. We have Asiatics in Vancouver, and there is no question about our being able to print story books, school books and professional and technical books in the languages of these people. When we have exhibitions we can invite these Asiatic people to come and see what we can do in Canada; and for goodness sake let us also go to them and ask them what they need. We have the paper and can do the printing with the greatest of ease. I think we could open up an unlimited market in Asia.
So far as the field of sport is concerned, there is no doubt that Canadians can produce the finest sporting equipment in the world. Our Olympic athletes have made a name for

Canada in hockey and skiing, and I think we should go to other countries, find out the type of sporting equipment they want and show them what we have.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to express certain views on the principle of Bill No. C-85, the purpose of which is to create a national design council. So far as design functions are concerned, my particular interest has been in connection with products made from nickel, and in that regard I might point out that an exhibition of stainless steel products was held about a year ago at the national gallery.
There is no doubt that the bill is welcomed by all members of the house, since its primary objective is to promote the sale of Canadian products and thereby increase Canadian production. In that regard it follows the ideals put forward by the government in past years, and a previous speaker has indicated quite well the efforts made in the past to formulate ways and means of promoting Canadian design.
I understand that at present there is a staff of 12 engaged in the promotion of Canadian design. However, in view of the growth of our country and having in mind our resources there is no doubt that a more complete and elaborate organization is needed to review the possibility of bringing about a greater incentive in Canada for the creation of designs that would be definitely Canadian and would result in our products being of a better quality.
The expansion of the functions of the national design council will certainly be appreciated by all hon. members and by the Canadian people. No doubt is was a shock to many Canadians to learn on a television broadcast the other day about certain problems that have arisen in recent years with respect to designing goods in Canada and the lack of proper promotion so they could be produced here. We were told, for example, about a plane required particularly for use in the northern areas of Canada which was designed here but could not be manufactured in Canada and had to be brought in from abroad. I urge the minister to give consideration to extending the objects of the council to include assistance in the promotion of Canadian produced goods.
On a previous occasion I referred to the ceremony at the opening of the national gallery, which was an elaborate and formal affair. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was hostess on that occasion and gave a splendid address. To my surprise most of the designs which won awards on that occasion were foreign. I am unable to give

an exact indication of the proportion of awards that went to foreign entries, because I did not expect to be speaking on this subject today. However, my impression is that very few of the outstanding, award winning designs were Canadian.
I was surprised, for instance, that an automobile produced in Europe won an award for stainless steel decoration. As a Canadian I regretted that an automobile manufactured or assembled in Canada had not won this award. As hon. members know, Canada produces a major portion of the world's stainless steel. I do not have current figures, but Canada's position in the production of monel metal would be even further advanced today as a result of Cuban production being curtailed.
No doubt people will be requested to sit on the council or its advisory committee without remuneration. This is a field in which we should obtain the highest possible degree of co-operation with industry. Although the council will bring benefits to the Canadian people generally it will bring particular benefits to industry. I urge that the minister strive to ensure that there will be in the council a high degree of co-operation with industry, and that consideration will be given to doing everything possible to assist in the promotion of Canadian products.
It should be brought to the attention of the public that many Canadian produced goods are superior in design and quality to imported goods. I hope the council will direct its efforts to this end. Recently I spoke to a person who brought to my attention the fact that many Canadian textiles are superior in design and quality to foreign made textiles. We are accustomed to thinking that imported textiles are superior to ours. Certainly imported textiles are given great publicity, and attention is directed to their alleged superior quality. The council should bring to the attention of domestic and foreign consumers the superior craftsmanship and quality of Canadian textiles and other goods.
Five or six years ago I attended a lecture at which the speaker proved to the audience that a Canadian manufactured refrigerator was superior to one manufactured in the United States, and that the additional $40 or $50 which was paid for the Canadian unit was compensated for by the fact that the Canadian unit contained material of a superior quality. It is information of this sort which the council must bring to the attention of the buying public.
We congratulate the minister on the forward step that this bill represents, and urge him to ensure that the council do everything possible to assist in the domestic and 90205-6-262J
National Design Council foreign sales of Canadian made products in terms of publicizing their outstanding qualities.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the house to lend my support to this bill and to congratulate our young and energetic Minister of Trade and Commerce on bringing this measure before us.
Many interesting ideas have been brought to our attention in the discussion of this measure to establish a national design council, and I am sure the council will find them of value in their deliberations. May I suggest that when selecting this council the minister give consideration to the selection of a representative from the field of agriculture. We have many food products in Canada which are of outstanding quality. I think particularly of Canadian cheese, maple syrup, hams, bacon and many other fine products. When travelling south of the border we often see reference made to Canadian bacon on the menus of restaurants. This is a field in which the council could promote Canada and Canadian products. I urge the council, through the minister, to bear this in mind and to have our Canadian foodstuffs of great distinction brought to the attention of people in other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make some more extended remarks, but unfortunately I was obliged to be absent from the chamber while the minister was making his speech on the motion for second reading of the bill. I think it is extremely necessary in our national life to get persons interested in form and in colour. There is a great deal in life beyond just the purely material, and the more people we can get interested in the purpose of this bill the better it will be. Ugliness is one of the factors contributing to many of our problems. People live in ugly surroundings; they use ugly equipment and ugly things. I am a great believer in the remedial effects of beauty in life.
I want to pay a tribute to those Canadians who do work in this field which is not generally known. There are some persons who make contributions to industrial and other designs across Canada. There are many more who are capable of making contributions if they have the opportunity to do so. I suggest that the council should inform the public on

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say very much about this bill in view of what has already been said. However, I wish to make one suggestion to the minister. I had the responsibility at one time, in a general way, along with the late Mr. C. D. Howe, for the design council as it exists at the present time. The question of whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce rather than the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should have the prime responsibility is not, in my opinion, a matter of great importance, although there is probably something to be said for relating the council more directly to industry, through putting it directly under the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whoever he may be, for the accomplishment of an immediate and intimate relationship between industry and the work of the council.
I feel that it would be only right to say what I am now going to say, and I do so particularly because I have a suggeston to make
[Mr. Herridge.l

to the minister. I would urge this suggestion on the minister. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most of us are parents I feel sure we all join in congratulating the hon. member for Peterborough and his wife on this addition to their family.
I should like to thank those hon. members who have spoken in this debate for the very constructive contributions they made. A great many good ideas have been put forward. I can assure the hon. members who made these suggestions that I and my departmental officials will take careful note of them, and

they will be brought to the attention of the design council once the members are chosen and the council set up.
The hon. member for Ottawa East and the hon. member for Niagara Falls voiced concern for the designers of Canada lest they be not protected by law regarding the designs they have worked on and produced. This protection continues to be provided for our designers through the Industrial Design and Union Label Act. When the present bill becomes law, as I hope it will, it will not in any way interfere with this protection. The purpose of this bill is solely to encourage good design in Canada.
The hon. member for Skeena asked whether a representative of organized labour could be included in the personnel of the council. The hon. member for Wellington South asked whether a representative of agriculture could be included. Although there are no specific categories for organized labour or agriculture on the council, section 3 (e) does provide for two people to be chosen from the general public. Of course representatives of labour, agriculture or any other category could be chosen to fill those vacancies.
I would stress that in choosing the personnel for this council we are particularly anxious to obtain people who are outstanding, who have done a great deal of work and study in the field of industrial design, and who are thereby able to make a really important and worth while contribution to improving design in this country. If hon. members know of people of particular talent in this regard, if they will let me know who they are and what their past work and experience has been I will be very glad to give them consideration.
I think it is particularly important that in the very competitive world in which we find ourselves today we should have products of outstanding Canadian design. I say this because in a market such as we have in Canada today, or the world market, which are both very competitive, to sell a product it must have either the best design, the best quality, or be offered at the lowest price. Sometimes it is necessary for a product to have a combination of two or three of these outstanding qualities. I think we have all had experience with products of outstanding design, and we know they usually command their own market and also a price well in excess of competitive products.
I should like to give four well known examples to illustrate this point. There is the machinery produced by the International Business Machines Corporation, the machines produced by the United Shoe Machinery Company-which produces machinery for manufacturing footwear-and the engines turned
National Design Council out for both automobiles and aeroplanes by the Rolls Royce Company. Also the fashions that are being produced by the world's top designers in Paris, New York, London and other fashion centres command their own markets at prices far in excess of those of their competitors.
I think the best way for producers in Canada to increase sales, and thereby increase the number of jobs available to Canadians, is to develop distinctive Canadian designs for our products. If we do this I feel we can win and hold markets at higher than competitive prices. If our design and quality are no better than that what is offered by those competing for our markets, then of course our producers will always be at the mercy of the price cutter and employment in these industries will be uncertain.
This is not the kind of situation we want in Canada. We want high and steady employment. The best way to make sure that we have both is to ensure that the products we produce will be asked for by name by people throughout the world as distinctive Canadian products, because they are better than the products offered by our competitors.
We have examples of that kind of design in certain of our agricultural products. I would name three that come to mind. One is Canadian cheddar cheese. Another is our No. 1 northern wheat. Another is Canadian bacon. Hon. members will know many others. These are products which have been developed by our agriculturists and which are well known throughout the world. These are asked for by name, and they have won for themselves an important place in the commercial market. I believe that if our agriculturists have been able to develop such outstanding products as these it is up to our industrialists to prove that they are just as able to develop unique Canadian products which can command their own markets and prices.
That is the real challenge facing Canadian industry today. It is to help industry meet this challenge that we are establishing the national design council, and I believe that working together to produce distinctive Canadian designs our industrialists, our workers and our manufacturers along with those interested in design throughout the country and those who are appointed to the industrial design council can help materially to increase the sales of Canadian products, thereby increasing the number of jobs available for Canadians.

Unfortunately I had to leave the chamber for three or four minutes during the time the minister was speaking, and if he did deal with this specific question and I missed his reply I am sorry. I apologize for being out of the chamber. Having had to leave the chamber myself for three or four minutes I sympathize with the hon. member for Skeena. While he was out I did answer his question. the inclusion of representatives of these two categories, there is in clause 3 subparagraph (e) provision for two people to be appointed from the general public, and representatives of labour and agriculture could well be included there. This would have to be decided later, but there would certainly be a possibility of that being done under the subclause.
I pointed out also that in choosing the members of the council we are particularly anxious to have people who have received special training and who have done special work in the field of design, in order that they may make a particular contribution to the work of the council. I invited hon. members to let me know any people who have done outstanding work in this field, because I should be glad to give consideration to their inclusion among the members of the council.

I do not know whether the minister was absent for the same reason as myself, but perhaps that is something we should not explore at this time. I understood the minister to say that representatives of agriculture and organized labour as well as, conceivably, of other elements in our society, could be appointed under subparagraph (e) where reference is made to two members of the general public. I also understood him to say that the government is anxious to have serving on this council people with special understanding of industrial design, or with special training in this field.
I think this is commendable, but I point out to the minister and to the committee that under clause 4, subclause (4)-and I refer to this, Mr. Chairman, only because it is connected with what I am about to say-it is provided that a person can only be eligible for appointment as a member of the council if he has knowledge of the field he is to represent or of the technical aspects of design. That is made clear in clause 3, subparagraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d). You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that the two members to be appointed under subparagraph (e) are specifically excluded from this obligation. Clause 4 says in effect that the two members of the general public need not have any knowledge of the design field or of the technical aspects of the work. If it is possible to appoint two members of the general public under paragraph (e) of this clause, one could conceivably come from the field of agriculture and another from the field of organized labour. That being so, why might they then be excluded from having technical knowledge in these particular fields, while it is required in respect of the other members?

Mr. Chairman, when members of the general public are included in a council they are usually included for the purpose of having additional points of view presented in discussions of the council, perhaps nontechnical points of view, or consumers' points of view. When I mentioned that representatives from the field of agriculture and organized labour could be included under clause 3, paragraph (e), I meant just that. It might be possible that those individuals chosen from the general public would be representatives of organized labour or agriculture. There would be no reason why they would not be. Who the individuals will be that are chosen I do not know, but I feel there is an opportunity for them there.

It seems to me that it would be desirable to have special reference to that effect included in this bill so as to ensure that the council will have representatives from the fields of agriculture and organized labour, in addition to the two members chosen from the general public. This would ensure that the consumers' point of view was represented as well as the points of view of the two large and important segments of our society, organized labour and agriculture. Those views would then be expressed within the council and would perhaps have some influence upon the council's recommendation.
I think it is necessary that I confine my remarks at this time to the representation by organized labour, but I would not like to be precluded from referring to that other important segment, agriculture. I feel that those members of this committee who are knowledgeable in regard to agriculture will be far more able to express points of view in that field than I am. In this regard I would like to place before the committee a motion along the lines I have suggested. I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, the following proposed amendment:

Mr. Chairman, with reference to clause 10 the objects are stated to be to promote and expedite improvement of design in the products of Canadian industry. Then it goes on to be more specific. It has recently come to my attention that it is most necessary that this be done in Canada. I have in mind crown corporations and particularly the Canadian National Railways, which very recently had recourse not to Canadian designers but rather American designers. I refer to an article published in October, 1960, indicating that Canadian National Railways has hired an American design group known as James Valkus, Inc. to do its entire corporate identity program, said to be the largest of its kind in North America. This company is an 11-man operation located in New York with a small branch office set up in Toronto specifically to accommodate this account. I think this indicates the fact that up until this time at least Canadian consumers including these branches of government, notwithstanding the council which has been in existence, have failed to take advantage of the excellent designers in Canada.
What is perhaps even more shocking is that those who use the hotel facilities of Canadian National Railways will find in their rooms a card of excellent design which I will be pleased to send to the minister. On one side it says "Please do not disturb" and on the other side it says "Maid please attend to

this room as soon as possible". It is a little plastic card of excellent design and very noticeable. At the top on one side appear the words "Canadian National Hotels" and at the top on the other side appear the words "Printed in the United States".
I think both these things should be a cause of shame to Canada. It is shameful that with respect to a small plastic card such as this Canadian National Railways has not been able to find Canadian designers or, if they have found them, have not purchased Canadian designs from them. It is particularly shameful that in the larger sphere of creating a whole corporate image it has been thought necessary by Canadian National Railways to go outside Canada and hire an American concern for this very large program.
I suggest to the minister that action in this regard is long overdue. It is a matter to which there should be much more attention paid, and the products of Canadian industry should be the primary concern of this council, not those of industries of other countries.

With regard to the use of Canadian design companies to assist other companies with their designs, I strongly urge all Canadian companies to make use of our own design companies, because this is the only way I know that our students who go through university and learn these arts and sciences can be employed in Canada instead of having to go to other countries for employment.

I am reading from clause 11, and I take it to mean the council will make recommendations to the minister in respect of the matters which the minister refers to it. Where is the provision, if there is one, to the effect that the council may make recommendations on all those maters which it undertakes of its own volition?

Well, Mr. Chairman, I think all those who listened to this debate would agree that one of the most important functions of the council is to automatically refer to the minister matters which it considers are of importance. I do not believe this function needs to be specifically set out. I can assure the hon. member for Skeena that when the council starts to operate there will be no doubt in the minds of the members of that council that I want referred to me any matters that they consider of importance or would like to refer to me. In fact I expect to be attending many of these meetings, because I am particularly interested in this matter myself. I assure the hon. member that there will be no lack of opportunity for the council to make its views known to me on any occasion upon which it wishes to do so. I will welcome those suggestions.

Then I feel that the bill should say so. If one refers to clause 11 of the bill one finds these words:
The council shall investigate and report on all matters referred to it pursuant to subsection 1-
That is pursuant to the minister's action.
-and shall make such recommendations to the minister in respect thereof as it deems appropriate.
Certainly I feel the council should undertake matters on its own volition, and there should be a similar statutory provision to enable the council to make recommendations and reports in respect of those matters.
