At that time I brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance three pamphlets that were written by an expert in the field of textiles. These pamphlets were afterwards sent to his parliamentary secretary at the minister's request. I shall not discuss that aspect, which is not germane at the moment, but there is one part of it which I think has reference to the design council. A suggestion was made at the time concerning the establishment of a textile council. I suggested to the minister that perhaps what I had in mind, namely some agency which would give consideration to improving the design of certain groups of textiles in Canada, might be given some consideration under the aegis of the productivity council or perhaps by the establishment of a textile council. The Primary Textiles Institute has since written to the press commenting on many of those things that were put on Hansard at the time, and stating that the Primary Textiles Institute, which has been in existence for some years, has been giving consideration to these very matters.
I rise this afternoon to point to one example which was given by the expert whose pamphlets I have given to the Minister of Finance, and to which I am sure the minister would want to give consideration after he has listened to what I have to say. This expert said it may well be that the design of some of our textiles has not been given the attention it should receive. For instance, he said there was a certain piece of woollen goods-he was referring to a sweater-that could be purchased in Switzerland at a cost of some $25 or $30. This sweater was akin to one which could be produced at La Mal-baie or Baie St. Paul for a much lesser amount, I think he said in the neighbourhood of $15. The wool is equally good, if not better, and the work is equally good, if not superior. However, the design does not compare with the design which was produced by the Swiss. It was his view that if the design of that particular commodity could be given to a group of experts who would work on it and make it more attractive, there would be a good demand for the article and it might not be necessary to import as many of these articles as we do.

I refer only, of course, to this particular item. The pamphlet I gave the minister dealt with many others. My only purpose in rising was to ask the minister if, when the council is established whose object will be to promote and expedite improved design for the products of Canadian industry, he would give consideration to these three pamphlets that are all ready in the hands of the Minister of Finance and according to which, in the opinion of this expert, if the design of Canadian textile goods were improved it could assist tremendously in the sale of those products not only in the province of Quebec but in the other provinces and the whole of Canada. I believe there are some 780 mills, mostly in central Canada but some in the west and some in the Atlantic provinces as well. My only purpose in rising is to ask the minister to be good enough to give this matter his careful consideration.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I will certainly do so. I am very keen about the matter which the hon. member for Laurier has raised. I have been told by a number of women that women's and children's clothes in this country, in the matter of design, do not come up to those produced in the United States and other countries, and lose out in the market for that reason and for that reason only. I am told they lose out not because of price but because of design.
I can well imagine the instance brought forward by the member for Laurier. That is just the kind of case that I should like to see this design council take hold of and help the manufacturers and the mills to which he referred produce an article of at least as good design as or, if possible, of better design than that produced in Switzerland and in that way get a much better market for the Canadian product. I thank the hon. member for Laurier for bringing this matter to my attention.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 10 carry?

There was one matter that I should like to mention with reference to subparagraph (g). The minister will recall, I think, that he attended a reception in the city of Ottawa about the end of last year at which an announcement was made with respect to a proposal to establish in Niagara Falls a permanent industrial exhibit. I should like to ask the minister whether, under this section, the design council will be responsible for participating in the sponsoring and arranging for such an exhibit showing particularly stylish displays of new Canadian materials in what is, after all, the foremost tourist centre in the whole dominion and a place which millions of people visit annually. It is perhaps the showcase in Canada for new 90205-6-263J
National Design Council and improved Canadian design. Is it anticipated that assistance-in a financial way, of course-might be given to such a permanent display under this particular clause?

No, not financial assistance. However, I feel sure that the council would encourage producers of certain light types of goods that could well be displayed at a centre of that kind to display their goods there. I am familiar with the particular centre about which the hon. member for Niagara Falls has spoken, because the mayor of Niagara Falls and a delegation came to see me about it several months ago. I was very much interested and assured them that I would give them all possible support and that I thought the idea was a good one. I still think so. I think it is a very forward looking step which the city of Niagara Falls is taking in this regard, and that the display centre will provide a very useful place for exhibiting Canadian products. More of this sort of thing is needed in Canada. I can assure the hon. member for Niagara Falls that we will give it every possible assistance.

While the hon. member for Niagara Falls was speaking I noticed that she is a woman of good taste. Everyone knows that women are noted for good taste. I wonder whether the minister should not consider the advisability of naming a woman as a member of this design council, and a young man as well. If you want to follow the fashion, you are usually young. Consider a man of my age for instance. I think the minister should consider the advisability of naming as members of the design council a woman and a young man.

There is no limit one way or the other as to the ages of these people we appoint to these councils. As I said earlier, we want to get the best possible people, those who can make a really worth-while contribution. In my experience young men and young women always make a good contribution to deliberations of this kind. I feel sure that young people will be represented on this council, having in mind the ability they have demonstrated in the past and the contribution we feel they could make to the work of the council. I might say that the lady representative on the productivity council, Miss Anna Speers, is making a good and useful contribution, and I feel sure that if there was a woman representative on this council she would make an equally good and useful contribution.

I wish to inquire of the minister about one other matter. This morning I mentioned certain things which the

National Design Council national industrial design council had proposed for this year, and particularly awards of merit in a competition that is to be decided in the fall of this year. Am I to understand that the work which is already in train under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will be carried on uninterrupted, at least until this program is completed, under this bill?
Yes, I am assured that any work that has already been started by the council will be carried on.
Is it anticipated that the same personnel will be carried over to the minister's department?
Yes, it is my understanding that is going to be done.
No, they have not been decided on. These are matters which the council itself will decide once it is set up.

Is it not the intention to follow the pattern that has been established by the existing design council in this matter? The minister must be aware that these awards have been made over the years and that a certain standard has come to be accepted for these things. I think it would be too bad to change that pattern.

Yes, it is our desire to carry on with the usual formula, but we are not limiting the work of the new council before it has been set up. It will, I feel sure, carry on the same general program. However, it must feel free to make whatever changes it, in its wisdom, considers are improvements.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 11-Reference to council.

Clause 11 has to do with what the minister may refer to the council, and provides that the council shall investigate and report on all matters referred to it in pursuance of subsection 1. I was wondering whether this council could be called on to report on products admitted to Canada bearing a Canadian design. I have in mind a number of products. One in particular has to do with salmon that was imported from Japan. A year or two ago I saw a number of cans of


salmon that bore the maple leaf design and on which in small letters appeared the words "Processed in Japan". I think this is pretty close to deception. People bought this salmon thinking they were buying salmon which had been processed in British Columbia. I should like to have the minister's comments on this subject.

These matters would not be examined by the design council itself, but they are of vital interest to my department. If the hon. member knows of an example such as he has mentioned, and would write me a letter about it, or if he prefers, discuss it with Mr. Dennis Harvey, the assistant deputy minister in charge of the commodities branch of my department, we will be very glad to look into the matter. These matters are looked after by the department itself, and not by the design council.

Mr. Chairman, we have had problems precisely the same as those related by the hon. member for Welland. We had this problem a few years ago, when salmon caught and packed in Japan was exported to Canada and sold under the labels of Canadian companies. The words "Produced in Japan" were printed along the side of the label, but so close to the gummed portion, which overlapped, that often the words "Product of Japan" were covered by the gummed portion of the label. But we did not deal with this matter through the Department of Trade and Commerce; it was dealt with through the Department of Fisheries. I wonder whether there is a conflict of activity here, or is it purely within the Department of Fisheries or the Department of Trade and Commerce?

Mr. Chairman, I can assure the hon. member for Skeena that we do not wish to overlap the jurisdiction of any other department. I think he and the hon. member for Welland will agree that the important thing is to have these matters dealt with efficiently and quickly.
Rather than direct the hon. member to other departments, if he will direct his inquiry or give any information that he has about this matter to my department, we will work with the Department of Fisheries. If it falls outside our jurisdiction, we will hand it over to them or any other department under whose jurisdiction it may come.
As the Department of Trade and Commerce, we are particularly interested to see that the kind of thing which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Welland should not continue.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one question on clause 11 (1), which states:
The minister may refer to the council for its consideration and advice such matters relating to the promotion and expedition of the improvement of design in Canada or otherwise relating to the operation of this act as he thinks fit.
My question is this. From what source would the minister accumulate information which he would refer to the council for consideration, as indicated in clause 11 (1)?

Mr. Chairman, a good example was given by the hon. member for Laurier a few minutes ago. The hon. member raised the example of sweaters that are manufactured in certain centres in Quebec and which sell at about half the price of sweaters imported from Switzerland. As the hon. member pointed out, the sweaters manufactured in Quebec are better made and are of better material. The only factor that mitigates against their ready sale as opposed to the Swiss article is that they are not as well designed.
I would refer a matter such as that, when brought to my attention, to the president of the design council and ask him to look into it, the idea being that if the mills in Quebec can be shown how they can improve their design, it is obvious that they will get a very much bigger market in Canada for their product.
I believe with a product of this kind we would develop an export market, because obviously the Swiss article is finding ready sales throughout the world-it is finding sales in Canada-and I would like to see the Canadian product moved into the world market and displace the Swiss article.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 12-Staff.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that the language of clause 12 (2) seems to be singularly indirect, to put it mildly. Apparently, if one reads it correctly-and I should like the minister to tell me whether I am reading it correctly-persons other than the officials of his department can be appointed to serve the design council, with the approval of the treasury board. But even Mr. Mackenzie King at his most deft could not have put it in a more negative way than it is put in this clause.
I should therefore like to know whether this clause does mean that if the design council is unable to find anyone in the Department of Trade and Commerce with sufficient leisure and sufficient capacity at the same time to perform the functions it needs, and if they can convince the minister that those functions
National Design Council are important, other persons can be employed for more than merely temporary periods or for specific work?

As I read the clause, it means that if the council needs additional help for temporary periods, which cannot be provided from within the government, it may acquire that help from outside the government, but it must first receive permission of treasury board to take on that extra help.
That is my interpretation of it, and I am assured by my official here that this is the correct interpretation. I am very glad it is. Therefore I am pleased to assure the committee that this is the interpretation.

In other words, it will not be possible to appoint anyone permanently; that is what the minister is saying.
Subclause (2) says:
-the minister may provide the council with such professional or technical assistance for temporary periods or for specific work-
I do not imagine the minister would embark upon specific work that was eternal. The minister is not going in for salvation in that sense. Therefore can we take it that there will be no permanent staff whatever for the design council except officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce?
Yes, that is correct; any staff will be provided from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister give the committee an idea of the number of persons and employees of his department who are at the present time or may be in the near future engaged in this work? What number does the minister contemplate?

I understand that there will be no more than about six on the staff at the present time. I am afraid I could not give an estimate as to the exact size of the staff that will be required once the council gets into full swing.

I have another question, Mr. Chairman. The minister says there are six members on the staff, or not more than six. I hope the minister knows how many there are, since he is spending the taxpayers' money.
He has just told you.
He said there were not more than six.
I am assured that there are six.

I should like to know the status of those people. Are they members of the staff of the Department of Trade and Commerce? If they are not, or if they do not

National Design Council become members of the department before this bill comes into operation, they will join the ranks of the unemployed?
They are members of the staff of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Could the minister say how and when they became members of the staff of the department? They certainly were not members of the staff of the Department of Trade and Commerce when the design council was under the national gallery.
Yes, they were transferred from the national gallery to the Department of Trade and Commerce some time ago.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 14-Financial.

Mr. Chairman, has the hon. minister some idea of what amount of money is intended to be expended? Is this to be increased over and above what has been spent in the past, in conformity with the statement the minister made this morning that there will be increased vigour and attention paid to this matter now?
Will there be any limit to the expenditure in this connection? I see there is apparently no limit to the expenditure that will be made, as there was in connection with the productivity council.

I am afraid I do not know what money is going to be required. When the council is set up and starts laying out its program, we will have some idea. I can assure the hon. member and all hon. members of this committee that money will not be wasted.
I cannot think of any better way in which money can be spent than by a council of this kind. It will operate at a very minimum of expense to the government. As the hon. member will have seen, there are no salaries paid to the members of this council. Their travelling and living expenses while away from their normal places of residence will be paid by the government. But I think when you consider the tremendous value that we get from groups of public spirited citizens such as those who will be making up this council, and who make up other similar councils which serve the government and the people of Canada, it will be seen that the government and the people receive tremendous service far out of proportion to the cost in dollars and cents.	.
I can assure the hon. member that expenditures on behalf of the government will be kept to a minimum and again I say I can think of no better way in which this money can be spent. I have here the figures for next year's estimates of what the industrial design

branch of my department will be spending but they have no relationship to the industrial design council itself. I can only say again that any expenditures made in this regard will, I think, be returned to the Canadian people many times over by increases in sales and the increase in employment which we hope will accrue from our being able to develop designs superior to any we have been able to develop in the past.

I am concerned about some of the specific objects set forth in clause 10. One has to do with making: grants or scholarships tO' individuals or institutions. Is it contemplated that the new council will have a large and expanded role in awarding scholarships to designers to study here and abroad? Has any consideration been given to how much money might be made available for such expenditures by the council?

These are all matters which will receive a great deal of study by members of the council when the council is operating, I have no idea what the council will recommend to me. We hope to; get very good people to serve on this council, people who are very keen and who know a great deal about design. I feel the recommendations they will make will be good and sensible ones and I can assure the hon. member that we shall study them carefully. We shall not go over board in connection with this matter and we shall agree to expenditures, only after a good deal of consideration, but just exactly what those expenditures are likely to be and how much they will amount to I cannot tell until the council has considered these matters and made recommendations to me.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 15-Report.

I have been comparing this bill with the bill which sets out the duties of the national productivity council. I am sure it is the intention of the minister to have the report of the design council included in the annual report of his department. However, the act setting up the national productivity council provides that the report of that council shall be tabled in parliament within 15 days of its receipt, I believe it is, or within 15 days of the opening of the next sitting of parliament. I wonder why a provision similar to that has not been included in this bill.

The productivity council is
allotted money of its own over which it has jurisdiction, specifically $150,000 a year. Any moneys that are expended by the national design council come directly from the Department of Trade and Commerce. When my estimates are being examined next year I shall be only too glad to answer any questions

regarding the expenditures or operations of the design council just as I would with regard to the operations of any branch of the department.

I wonder if it really is connected with whether or not the productivity council has finances of his own while this council operates through the funds and staff of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Surely there are other factors. 1 read in the act which sets up the national productivity council, or more correctly, from the bill which was placed before this house, that the chairman of the council is required within three months after the termination of each fiscal year to submit to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Minister of Labour a report of all the proceedings carried out under the act for that fiscal year, including the financial statement of the council. Thus, the productivity council has two subjects upon which to report. The financial operations for that year are included, and then there are the other proceedings. It would seem to me that a sensible course would be to require the chairman of the council to submit to the minister a report of the operations of the council within three months after the termination of each fiscal year, an obligation similar to that which is placed upon the chairman of the productivity council in accordance with the act to which I have just referred. Why should such a report not be tabled in parliament together with reports of other councils and agencies, crown corporations and the like?

Other crown corporations and boards are voted specific sums of money and they operate more or less independently. This council will derive its money directly from the department. Its staff will be members of the Department of Trade and Commerce and it will derive from the department itself any money which needs to be expended. It will therefore be in the same position as a section of my department. It is not given a block of money and told to go ahead and operate. It operates in a different way and, as I say, at the end of each year when my departmental estimates come before the committee of the whole I should be glad to answer any questions and give any accounting that is asked for regarding this council. There will be no concealment from members of the committee of any activities or expenditures. They will be able to fully examine those expenditures by asking me questions and I shall be glad to answer them. I hope I have made that clear.

The minister has made that part of it clear, but I do not think his answer completely covers the point I raised. Let us
Bras d'Or Coal Agreement consider the workings of the department over which the minister formerly had the honour to preside, the Department of Transport. That department looks after the Canadian maritime commission which makes a separate report, and yet the commission receives money voted by parliament to the Department of Transport. The penitentiaries branch of the Department of Justice also comes to mind. That is a separate branch within the Department of Justice and it makes a separate report, though its sole income is that voted by parliament. Consider, also, the position of the director of research and investigation in connection with the Combines Investigation Act. He receives funds from the Department of Justice. The combines branch has no money of its own other than that which comes from the department, yet a separate report is made. Here are two or three instances which come to mind immediately of bodies which receive money only as voted by this house, yet they make reports which are tabled in parliament.
Mr. Chairman, I am asking why the report of this council will not be tabled in the house. I am not referring to any attempt by the minister to hide anything. I think we all realize that the minister will, as he has assured us, answer any questions we wish to put forward but I am wondering why this report will not be tabled.

As the hon. member knows, the Minister of Trade and Commerce issues a report of his department's activities each year. Included in that report will be a report of the industrial branch of my department, and as part of its report there will be the report of the industrial design council. All hon. members will receive a report of the activities of this branch and of the industrial design council each year in booklet form as part of the total report on the activities of my department.
That is the answer to the question I asked in the first place.

Clause agreed to.
Title agreed to.

Bras d'Or Coal Agreement
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize certain amendments to the agreement made under the Coal Production Assistance Act with the Bras d'Or Coal Company Limited for the purpose of postponing the commencement of repayment of the loan made to the company thereunder to the 31st day of December, 1962.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AGREEMENT WITH BRAS D'OR COAL COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this bill is to permit the company-the Bras d'Or Coal Company Limited situated at Broughton, Nova Scotia, not far from North Sydney-to defer payment of moneys loaned under the Coal Production Assistance Act. That act provides that repayments shall be made at the rate of 30 cents per ton on coal produced. The company used the money provided to buy a specialized mining machine intended specifically to increase efficiency and production. The repayment would come, in large part, from the coal produced by this machine.
In early 1959 there was an unexpected fall of ground in the mine which cut off the area where this machine and others were operating. This not only reduced the production on which the repayment was based but also forced the company to secure new machinery and spend considerable capital on a new approach to the affected area.
At the present time, the new workings have almost reached the buried machines, but it will take some time before they can be taken out of the mine, inspected, put back into operating condition, and replaced in the mine. They will not, therefore, be available for producing coal on which to base repayment, until this is completed. Because of this accident, and to conserve the working capital position, the company has requested postponement of the first repayment date to December 31, 1962 without deferment of the date on which, under the act, the final payment is due.
I must also say, Mr. Chairman, that this company obtained the first loan early in 1959 for the purpose of buying machinery to increase its production. The accident happened, the company had to stop operations, and was forced to apply for a new loan. The first loan has been regularly paid under the conditions of the loan in the amount of $14,000. Repayment has not taken place yet regarding the second loan and the company is now asking to defer the first instalment for two years.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO AGREEMENT WITH BRAS D'OR COAL COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the light of the explanation given by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, I do not think that I, or any of my friends on this side of the house, would be prepared to argue that this bill, by itself, does not represent the expedient thing to do under the circumstances.

I must say that I feel rather sorry for the minister in having to introduce this bill at this particular time, but because of the fact that this bill really preserves the working capital of this particular company and enables it to go on with its operations it must be doubly comforting to the minister in the light of the unpleasant news that he undoubtedly read in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of April 28 under the large red headlines "Dosco Files Formal Notice-Glace Bay Mine to Close May 31". I do not intend to go into this in any detail but we do know now that it appears that three mines are going to have to be closed in Cape Breton this year unless the federal government is able to find some means of doing something about the situation.
There is no doubt that what the minister is doing now is taking one tiny nibble-not even a bite-at a problem which is so vital to the interests of one of the ten provinces of Canada that it is in every respect a national problem amounting to a crisis.
I feel that in saying anything about this particular measure that the government is proposing to bring in, one cannot help but say that it would have been more expedient if the government had come forward with- perhaps not a solution to the problem because I do not think the government, or anyone else at this time, has any assurance of a solution-but some steps to be taken to make sure that these mines are not closed or-

speechtext:
On the point of order raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, I would agree that if we were on the bill, of which we only have notice here, it would be quite inappropriate to discuss anything except the principle of the bill. But what we are doing here, and this has often been discussed before on points of order at the committee stage of a financial resolution, is to decide Whether or not a particular sum of money should be spent out of the treasury.
I say, sir, without any fear of contradiction, even by hon. gentlemen opposite, that this is one area where it would be more expedient-I follow the language as nearly as I can-to spend more money out of the treasury in order to avoid what in my opinion will be something closely approaching a national calamity. It is on that basis that I

feel what I have been saying is quite appropriate. I would think it would not be appropriate to embark upon a general debate on the coal industry, but all I intended to do was to suggest in a very brief sort of way how an alternative resolution would be much more acceptable to certain members of the committee than the resolution we have before us. I grant you, sir, that I am under certain limitations in doing so. I am a member of the opposition and while it is true that I happen to be one of Her Majesty's privy councillors I am temporarily unemployed in that capacity. Unfortunately, however, there are many of Her Majesty's subjects who are going to be unemployed for a very long time if we do not grapple with the problem in Cape Breton in a more effective way than this resolution does.
Everyone agrees that we cannot mine coal just to build it into mountains. The minister did try that for a while and he became discouraged with that policy. I must say I should like to congratulate the minister, the coal board and everyone in the federal government who had any part in convincing Ontario hydro that they should use some of this coal. I am sure the minister was quite cheered up by that as was everyone who has at heart the interests of the people of that area. But there again, sir, one wonders whether it would not be more satisfactory to be generating electricity with that coal in Nova Scotia and using it in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not know at what point the hon. member stopped discussing the point of order but I am quite sure it was some time ago. I must say I have not been convinced by his argument that because we are at the resolution stage we can discuss any alternative proposal in the way he put it. I think the subject before the committee as outlined by the resolution is a very limited one. The resolution refers only to postponing the commencement of repayment of a loan because of a certain accident. Therefore I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that under such circumstances we are not permitted to discuss the coal situation in general. I felt that the hon. member could make some passing references to it but now I think he is going further than that.

In that case, sir, I shall be obliged, I suppose, to point out reasons why I do not think it is expedient to proceed with this resolution at this particular moment. I am sure Your Honour would not object to my taking that line of argument. I do not think it is expedient to proceed with this resolution until the government has laid before us a program to deal with the much larger
Bras d'Or Coal Agreement and more serious problem which is imminent in Cape Breton at the present time. I say that for many reasons, not the least of which is the fact that the house is sitting very long hours and that we could economize on the time of the house if the government had brought in one single resolution dealing with the whole problem instead of taking this piecemeal approach to the problem.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

Is it the hon. member's intention in putting forward this argument that the smaller operations in Cape Breton should be sacrificed while at the same time the government is making every effort to maintain the larger operations? Is the hon. member going to vote for this measure? Does he consider that the smaller operator also has to be taken care of?

At the conclusion of my remarks I will be very happy to answer the question of the hon. member for Cape Breton South who, I am sure, is just as much concerned as I am with the well-being of the coal miners. As I was saying, it does seem to me that it would have been more expedient at this time, when the problem has already become urgent, to have brought in a resolution, to have dealt with the real problem of the area. Although the problem involved in the resolution now before us is one which ought to be dealt with and, it seems to me, is perhaps by itself being dealt with in the right way, it is nevertheless a very minor problem.
If at the same time the government could have brought in its resolution indicating what it proposes to do about the closing of mines in Cape Breton and, above all, what it proposes to do to provide not just relief but alternative employment for the people in this historic area of our country, it seems to me we would have been able to accept this resolution with a good deal more satisfaction than is possible having regard to the unfortunate circumstances which prevail at the present time and about which, I regret very much to say, the ministers seem to have nothing to propose.

The first of them is the extent of the dependence of Nova Scotia upon coal. There is no counterpart in the economy of any other province to this degree of dependence.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a short statement to make in connection with the proposed bill. The Army Benevolent Fund Act was passed in 1947 to establish a fund for the benefit of those who served in the Canadian army during world war II.
During the war extensive services were performed for the troops by various agencies, including several auxiliary services organized
4170	HOUSE OF
Army Benevolent Fund Act in Canada and the navy, army and air force institute, in the benefits of which the Canadian forces participated.
The moneys accumulated by these services, and some additional funds which became available from sales on troopships and the sales of kitchen by-products, were gathered together and added to the moneys remaining in the regimental funds of army units. The total amount of all these moneys was somewhat over $9 million.
The act of 1947 established the army benevolent fund board for the administration and distribution of these funds. Since that time the board has continued to operate in a satisfactory way with the assistance of provincial committees, and up to March 31, 1960, distributed nearly $6 million. In their endeavour to continue the measure of assistance which was originally contemplated, the expenditures from the fund have so far been somewhat greater than planned.
In 1952, in order to help this situation some assistance was given by increasing the rate of interest payable on the fund. If hon. members wish to refer to that earlier debate, they will find it in Hansard for June 10, 1952, on page 3108.
The main proposal of the present bill recognizes the same problem, together with the well-known fact that rates of interest have been consistently higher than now authorized by this legislation. Therefore an increase of one half of 1 per cent is proposed.
This would increase the rate payable to 4 per cent per annum to the extent that the minimum balance of the fund does not exceed $5 million, and 3 per cent per annum to the extent that the minimum balance exceeds $5 million.
The estimated annual cost to treasury of this proposed amendment is $32,000, which will of course reduce as time goes on. The opportunity has also been taken to include two comparatively minor administrative amendments to the act which are found to be desirable.
The first of these is to allow the army benevolent fund board to set the salary of the secretary of the board. The salary of $6,500 a year now contained in the act was set in 1947 and has never been changed. In the interval there have been a number of general salary increases throughout the civil service, and it is thought only appropriate that the salary of this officer should not be restricted as it is at present. The board now has the authority to incur other administrative expenses, including salaries for its other employees.
The second minor amendment deletes from section 11 of the act a requirement which does not now and in fact never did exist.


When the administrative organization serving the board was originally contemplated, it was expected that the provincial committees would handle funds and that their accounts would be audited on a local basis. That has not been followed and all auditing is done centrally in Ottawa.
This portion of the section is non-effective and the proposal is to drop it, following a suggestion made by the Auditor General.
Mr. Chairman, that constitutes a brief introduction to the bill. As with other bills which come under the veterans charter, it is the intention, if the house approves, to refer the measure to the standing committee on veterans affairs after second reading for further consideration. Consequently at this time perhaps this committee does not want to go into too great detail with regard to this particular fund. Following the resolution stage and first reading the bill will be distributed and it should be available for consideration on second reading tomorrow. If second reading is given, the matter will be referred to the committee on veterans affairs and in due course it will come back to the house.
I commend this measure to hon. members. It will give the fund more money for a very essential service which it has been performing for veterans who need special assistance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I rise to indicate our support for this resolution and I should also like to take advantage of this opportunity to pay tribute to the army benevolent fund board and the work they have done and are doing. As the minister said, the board was established by an act of this parliament in 1947. Prior to that the fund had been administered by the regimental funds board who reported to parliament through the minister of defence. This change was brought about by a recommendation of a special parliamentary committee set up in February, 1947.
The bill establishing the army benevolent fund board was drafted by that special parliamentary committee and appended to its report to parliament-a very rare if not unique event. This bill provided that the fund should be administered by a board and it stipulated that at least one member of the board should be nominated by the royal Canadian legion and another by the national council of veterans' associations. No member of the board was to occupy any position in the public service of Canada. The bill also provided for a veterans welfare program and in 1953 the army benevolent fund board worked out a second program jointly with the board of directors of the Canadian army welfare fund. This program was approved by the cabinet in 1953 and became known as the Canadian army financial welfare program.

Under these two programs assistance has been given to veterans and their dependents, to the widows and orphans of deceased veterans and to second world war veterans who are still serving in the Canadian army. The type of assistance rendered is mainly of a kind intended to meet unexpected contingencies and to help veterans and their families out of various financial difficulties.
Included among these activities have been arrangements to have debts adjusted and orderly repayment made when the debts have been incurred for justifiable reasons. In addition the board has set up a counselling service which has assisted veterans' families in budgeting and money management.
Another service has been rendered to unemployed veterans. In these cases no direct relief can be given but the special employment program of the army benevolent fund board helps veterans in relocating to places where jobs are available and in retraining them and supplying them with tools of the trade. These activities have been co-ordinated with the work done by the Canadian naval service benevolent fund and the R.C.A.F. benevolent fund. Many worthy families have been saved from financial disaster and restored to a sound economic footing as a result of this work.
The funds which are being administered originated, as the minister has told us, mainly through canteen profits but they have also been augmented from other sources because many large camps had various enterprises attached to them such as theatres, curling rinks, bus services and so on all of which provided profits which would contribute to the general fund. As the minister has also told us, the original amount in 1947 was $8,134,934. It was expected that another million dollars would be added, making approximately $9 million.
On March 31 last the fund had declined to $6,863,020. The purpose of this bill, as the minister has just said, is two fold. In the first place it seeks to increase to 4 per cent the rate of interest being paid on the fund and it also seeks to make provision for certain changes in administration. We fully agree with the principle of both these changes and intend to support the resolution.

I rise on behalf of this group to support the purpose of this resolution. I am not saying, however, that we shall be altogether satisfied with the bill when it is introduced.
It is interesting to look back to the year 1947. I was a member of the special committee on veterans affairs which dealt with this legislation, in particular, at that time, as mentioned by the previous speaker. Shortly
Army Benevolent Fund Act after the act came into effect a total of something over $9 million was available to the fund. Last year, according to an excellent report submitted by Mr. Chatterton to the standing committee on veterans affairs, we were informed that the board had completed 12 years of operation of the veterans welfare program as provided for in the Army Benevolent Fund Act and seven years of operation of the Canadian army welfare program as provided for in the arrangements between the board of directors of the Canadian army welfare fund and the army benevolent fund as approved by the cabinet in 1953. As mentioned by the previous speaker, we were told that the fund had been reduced to something less than $7 million.
Throughout the years there have been certain suggestions made with respect to assistance in the administration and in recent years it has been the practice for the government to grant $18,000 a year toward the administrative costs of the army benevolent fund. We were told that the average amount of the grants was in the nature of half a million dollars a year and from personal experience I know of the excellent work which has been done by the board. This fund has served a very useful purpose indeed. In fact, on a number of occasions of which I am aware it has proved a virtual life saver to the veteran concerned.
I was very interested last year when it was brought to our attention that a veteran, who was in rather deep water, felt that if he could be granted sufficient money to purchase a horse he could skid logs and get out of debt. The board provided the money, he was able to skid the logs, and he finally got back on his feet. I would suggest this is an example of the purpose of the fund. I know of numerous cases where this fund has been of great advantage to veterans who found themselves in difficult circumstances. In view of the good work enabled by this fund, it is natural on our part to want to see that the fund is continued as long as possible, commensurate with meeting needs and circumstances of the day.
I must say that as a result of our experience after the first world war, in regard to other funds, this fund has been administered on a very sound, practical and humane basis. Originally, as I understood it, interest was set at 2J per cent which, in the light of the circumstances at the time the fund was established, as the hon. member for Essex East would say, seemed very reasonable indeed. It was later found necessary to increase the interest, and I understand the interest is now 3J per cent on the first $5 million and 3 per cent on the balance. This resolution, without doubt has been brought to

Army Benevolent Fund Act the attention of the committee by the minister as the result of certain prodding of the government by those individuals who felt that the fund should earn more interest in view of present circumstances. I know that officials of the royal Canadian legion and the national council of veterans have had this in mind. I am quite sure from reading the reports of the army benevolent fund over the years that in recent years the officials of that organization felt there was complete justification for increasing the interest rate at this time and thereby the earning power of the fund which would in turn extend its life.
There is no mention of a specific interest rate in this resolution. Governments have the habit of sort of pulling the rabbit out of the hat later on and we will look forward to seeing what is in the hat. However, I do suggest in view of present circumstances, and because of the fact that loans are being made at 5 per cent, we could very well establish an interest rate of 5 per cent in respect of the army benevolent fund to make certain that the fund is kept in existence as long as possible. We look forward to reading the bill when it is brought forward in the house.
One other amendment I suggest we could look for in this resolution would be an amendment granting the benefits of the army benevolent fund to Newfoundland veterans. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in looking over the annual report to March 31, 1960 of the army benevolent fund I see the names of


the chairman, the four members of the board, the members of the nine provincial special committees including all the provinces except Newfoundland, and one overseas committee, and I would like at this time to pay tribute to the chairman, the members of the board and the members of those special committees for the good work they have been doing. I have seen some evidence of this while practising medicine.
This fund was set up in 1954 to incorporate the management of the army canteen fund and other service funds. They were all brought under the one act. At that particular time the interest rate was 2J per cent paid on the whole amount. In 1952 the act was amended in respect of interest only. According to that amendment the interest on the fund was set at 3J per cent on the first $5 million and 2J per cent on the balance. The minister has said today that the proposed interest rate would be up one half of one per cent in both cases. This will mean that the highest interest rate possible is 4 per cent. The government certainly cannot borrow money at an interest rate lower than 5 per cent today, which is 1 per cent higher than the highest proposed interest rate in respect of this fund. The previous government paid an interest rate very much closer to the interest rate on the market at that time.
Originally the board was guided by certain principles, one being that there would be prospective beneficiaries for 50 years. In 1958 and 1959 the fund was depleted by over $300,000 per year. Last year the fund was depleted, as at March 31, 1960, by $317,000. If the fund is depleted at this rate it will soon not exist at all. I am not criticizing the management of the fund but am calling this situation to the attention of this committee. Unless there is some extra money put into this fund, and if it is depleted at the rate of approximately $320,000 per year, it will soon be gone. It was suggested when the fund was set up that it would run for some 40 more years. I notice now that there is some $6 million with the government, and over $250,000 in conversion loans at 4J per cent due in 1983, and the fund has already taken a loss of something over $30,000 in respect of these bonds at present market values.
I should like to ask the minister who controls these funds. Does the board have control or does he or does the Minister of Finance? I have often wondered about that. I know that there are several other funds in existence. Probably conversion loan bonds were also bought by those funds and I should like to know whether or not they also suffered losses. I do not suppose the minister can answer that question at this time.

I think the board is doing excellent work. As I said before, a number of very worthy cases have come to my notice. The fund is also in the lending field, and I was surprised to learn the amount of money that has been lent to veterans and the small losses that have been sustained. After we see the bill we will be able to discuss the matter further.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have nothing particularly edifying to say today with respect to the resolution but I cannot let pass this opportunity to make a few comments about the fund. In the brief time I have been in the house only one matter has come before the fund in which I have been concerned. I have been asked to indicate not only the approval of the recipients with respect to the action of the fund but also of a great many veterans in the area and veterans organizations.
The army benevolent fund is perhaps not too well known to the general public and not as well known to veterans as it might be. The particular case which came to my attention concerned a veteran with an exceptionally fine war record who had suffered a very debilitating disease. He has a wife and small children of school age and these people were absolutely incapable of meeting even the hospital and medical accounts. This woman came to me in sheer desperation after she had been every place where she thought she might conceivably obtain assistance. The matter was referred to the directors of the army benevolent fund in Ontario who with a minimum of red tape, which I think is most unusual in matters that are the responsibility of the government, and great consideration for the feelings of the people involved and the record of the veteran, took over the payment of these accounts. This had a most beneficial effect with respect to the wife and the children because the children were able to remain at school and the wife was able to carry on with their support. However, perhaps even more important, so far as the veteran himself is concerned, the provision of assistance has enabled him to be freed of financial responsibility and of worry so far as his family and his own future are concerned.

As a former member of an army mess, I think the fund could not be put to better use. Those of us who served in second war as well as those who served in the first war are happy

These are the sources of the funds about which we are talking and, as I mentioned at the start, they were derived as a result of the activities of our second world war army veterans.

They know at first hand, as we all do, of cases of valuable assistance which has been rendered by the fund. However, as far as the statistical record is concerned, I should like to point out that from September, 1957, to March, 1960, the fund made financial grants amounting to $4,691,131. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-84, respecting the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons and the co-ordination of rehabilitation services.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of this legislation is to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with

the provinces respecting support for their efforts to develop a comprehensive and coordinated program of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons. It is an honour for me to be associated with legislation, the high purpose of which is to help ensure that thousands of our disabled citizens will have more useful lives.
As was expected, hon. members from all parties endorsed the purpose of this bill when they spoke at the resolution stage. Wherever possible it is more desirable, more beneficial and more humane to restore the disabled to vocational usefulness than to support them in demoralizing dependency. I want to thank hon. members who have spoken on this subject. They have obviously studied the present situation, and in doing this they must have realized that under present provisions, securing the various services necessary to the vocational rehabilitation of the disabled can be a baffling and time consuming process. I feel, and I am sure we all feel, it is time to remove much of the confusion surrounding this field.
I feel we must pave the way for the development of an orderly, co-operative and co-ordinated pattern of vocational rehabilitation. With such a pattern, and assured of federal support, the provinces will be able to plan expansion of their programs with vigour and imagination, resulting in greatly increased federal financial participation.
In presenting the resolution to the house a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, I did not claim- I should like to make this perfectly clear- that this government had invented vocational rehabilitation nor, of course, do I lay any claim that it was invented by the previous administration. The whole concept and philosophy have developed gradually over a great many years. The principles were first practised in Canada on a large scale after the first world war. Some of our provincial workmens' compensation boards were quick to grasp the value and the common sense of this approach to the problem of the severely disabled. Our voluntary agencies were similarly inspired. Other progressive nations introduced constructive measures to develop comprehensive programs of vocational rehabilitation.
In spite of this, it was not until 1951 that a national conference was called on the subject here in Canada. It was not until 1953 that a limited degree of financial support was made available to the provinces to encourage the development of rehabilitation as a co-ordinated and co-operative effort. The steps taken at that time, I feel and I am sure everyone will agree, have been useful. They provided a basis for experiment. The experiment has resulted in a degree of success which has

confirmed our belief in the basic principles of vocational rehabilitation. However, in operation, weaknesses that required correction have been revealed.
At the eighth world congress on rehabilitation held last year in New York, a prominent Canadian made this statement to the representatives of 60 nations. I should like to quote his words:
I know of few fields In which the problems of organization and administration of a program are so complex and as baffling as they are in the field of rehabilitation.
In a program in which so many divisions and levels of government, so many professional disciplines, and so many voluntary groups are involved, the authority for the program must be clear as to its intent. The administrative framework must be as simple as is possible in a complicated situation. When we are dealing with the provinces in a proram designed to bring services to individuals, it is much easier for them to develop these programs against the background of a statute that is clear in its purpose.
At present, in recovering the federal share of the costs of supplying vocational rehabilitation services, the governments of the provinces must do so through two separate federal departments. Administration will obviously be simplified and made possible by this bill, that is Bill No. C-84. It will only be necessary for the provincial rehabilitation authority to make recovery through one federal department. The national advisory committee on the rehabilitation of disabled persons has repeatedly asked the government to consider the possibility of legislation in this field. I now have every reason to believe that this bill will be met with a great deal of satisfaction by all the provinces across Canada. It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that in close cooperation with my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith), this measure has been drawn up.
The basic purpose of this bill is to authorize the making of agreements with the provinces to provide for the sharing of costs incurred by the provinces in carrying out programs of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons. The title of the bill is "The Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act". The definitions indicate the segment of the population that we seek to benefit and the types of services that may be necessary in a program of vacational rehabilitation.
To implement the provisions of the bill the minister will be authorized, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into an agreement with any province for a period not exceeding six years. These federal-provincial agreements will provide for financial assistance for costs incurred by the prov-
Vocational Rehabilitation ince in implementing a comprehensive program for the rehabilitation of disabled persons. The agreement will set out how, and in what manner, various provisions of restoration, training and employment placement may be made available to the disabled. The principal services for which costs may be shared are outlined.
The vocational rehabilitation of the individual must be based upon adequate counselling and a proper assessment of his potentialities. Where full employment is not possible, economic gain can be sought by assisting the seriously disabled to dispense with institutional care or the services of an attendant. The desirability of training staff as counsellors or administrators is quite obvious. Such staff is essential to the proper co-ordination of services and bringing them to the disabled individual as required in an orderly, organized manner. Additional services that may be necessary may be included as required in individual cases. As an example, we could share the cost of tools without which employment could not be accepted.
The responsibility of co-ordinating federal services that relate to vocational rehabilitation is placed with the Minister of Labour in co-operation with the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Department of National Health and Welfare, working with provincial health departments, is responsible for the development of all those services and facilities required to meet the health needs of our people. This responsibility includes the encouragement of the maximum use of all treatment measures conducive to complete cure or maximum recovery.
The health grants, and particularly the medical rehabilitation and crippled children grant, have stimulated the expansion of physical medicine and medical rehabilitation facilities in hospitals and rehabilitation centres. Equipment has been supplied, staff has been trained. These services speed up recovery and reduce the eventual degree of permanent disability. The creation of facilities and services, and the setting of standards in this area are, and must always be, the responsibility of our medical people.
Authority is given to the Minister of Labour to carry out research as it relates to vocational rehabilitation, where appropriate, in cooperation with any province.
The duties of the national advisory council on the rehabilitation of disabled persons are clearly set out. Its purpose basically is to give consideration to and advise the minister on all questions relating to the operation of the act. In addition to the federal and provincial representatives, the council will draw its ten

Vocational Rehabilitation remaining members from labour, management, the medical profession, the universities and the national voluntary agencies that work with the disabled.
To ensure that when purchasing medical services for individuals this is done in harmony with the developing pattern of health services, all regulations for this area will be recommended jointly by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
It can be seen, therefore, that the measure sets out specifically the responsibilities of the federal government in this important field. The resulting agreements will enable the provinces to indicate the services that they are willing to provide. This in turn should enable the provinces and the voluntary agencies to work out a co-ordinated approach in which the role of each in a total rehabilitation program is understood and defined.
This is not primarily a training program. Vocational training is an important part, but only one part, of vocational rehabilitation. Where training is given, it is based upon the abilities and desires of the individual and the opinion of the national employment service as to whether or not such training should lead to placement. The national employment service works closely with provincial rehabilitation offices, and I am proud of the fact that they have, in the past years, placed thousands of disabled persons in jobs that they are well able to perform.
It should be noted that under this vocational rehabilitation program, costs are not assumed for services that are generally available to all citizens under other programs. This is necessary to avoid overlapping. Where a voluntary agency can provide one of the necessary services, they assume this responsibility. The whole success, however, depends upon a well organized process through which the disabled can be guided to assume their rightful place in our economy.
Money is not actually spent on rehabilitation. It is invested, I submit, in order to provide a better future for our disabled citizens and the dividends that are returned in their greater happiness and their increased contribution to the economy more than offset the initial cost.
I am sure that all members of this house and of the entire nation will welcome this expression of our basic belief in the true principles of democracy and the provision, as far as possible, of equal opportunity for all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill will put into statute form authorization for the government to enter into agreements with the provinces on a cost

sharing basis to co-ordinate all federal activities in the field of vocational rehabilitation. It will also provide for all co-operative work with the provinces in that field, including medical, surgical and remedial treatment as well as research in these fields. It will also provide for the setting up of an advisory council and authorize the payment of a chairman and other expenses.
As was said in the house the other day, there is nothing actually new in this bill except that henceforth payments in respect of helping the handicapped will be classed as statutory expenditures instead of a vote in the estimates. Every year when this vote in the estimates has come up for consideration in the committee, the minds of hon. members have been focused on the handicapped and they have had the opportunity to discuss the matter in debate and to bring their opinions to the attention of the government. I know that the minister said-and he repeated it today-that this is not something new; but when he brought this measure into the house at the resolution stage I think he left the impression that there was something in it when he used these words:
-it will bring new hope and encouragement to many of our less fortunate citizens.
I think we can see that those words are not, in fact, true for the fact is that our handicapped people will have available to them now nothing that they did not have available previously under the votes in the estimates.
I recall that back in 1954 when this measure was first introduced in the house, it and similar measures had no greater sponsor and advocate in the house than the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). At that time the hon. member was minister of national health and welfare. I have heard him sponsor this and similar measures in the house on various occasions. I say that no one in this house has been more active than he in sponsoring social security measures.
As the minister said, helping the handicapped started by a vote in this house in 1954. On the resolution stage of this bill the other day the minister gave some statistics. I think he said 5,266 seriously disabled people had been helped. They had over 3,000 dependents, and 80 per cent of them were without earnings.
Instead of being a charge to the taxpayers of Canada to the amount of $3.9 million a year, these people have been able to earn up to $9.6 million a year after rehabilitation. They have earned a total of $29 million since rehabilitation. I think this is evidence enough that this program was started at an earlier time under the former government.

Many people who are physically handicapped will receive the benefit of advances in medical science. Much has been done in the field of orthopaedic surgery. Much can be done to help those with defects in vision. Also, with the new braces and new artificial limbs I think these people can be helped a great deal more. Many of them have been helped a great deal so far.
The minister said this bill was being introduced in order to give assurance to the provinces that this program will be carried on. I did not think it was necessary for us to give any further assurance to the provinces than we have in the past. However, if anybody in the provinces needs any assurance, this is it.
Many advances are being made in medical science and we want to continue to help the physically handicapped. Therefore I think everybody in this house should vote for this bill.

Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage the representative of this group expressed support for the principle of the bill it was proposed to introduce. We are naturally very pleased to now see the actual bill and therefore obtain a greater understanding of its purport, how far it will go and just what it is that the government has in mind. Undoubtedly the principle of the bill is good and its effects will be far-reaching.
As has been pointed out by the minister, in these days it is possible, with modern science and teaching, to recognize the great possibilities that exist for the rehabilitation of those persons who have become disabled.
Through the past operations of workmen's compensation boards in this country and the activities of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, we have seen just what can be done in the rehabilitation of those who have become physically disabled. Because of that experience we very much welcome the introduction of this bill which will make statutory a policy of assisting the provinces to help the disabled throughout this country.
We fully understand that the particulars of the bill make it necessary for the initiative to be taken by the provinces and for agreements to be reached between the provinces and the federal government as to the scope of the rehabilitation measures.
We in this group sincerely hope that all provinces will take the fullest possible advantage of this legislation and that the federal council which is to be established, and the minister who has the responsibility, will have a broad vision as to the potentialities of the principle of rehabilitation.
I hope that during the course of the discussion on this bill the minister will outline,
Vocational Rehabilitation in perhaps more detail as we discuss the various clauses of the bill, what he considers to be some of the problems which have to be met and what he considers to be the breadth and scope of the bill.
The reason I mention this is because in days not so long past a person who had lost an arm, both arms, or a leg might not-and most certainly could not, I would say-be able to adapt himself for other occupations through vocational training because of the type of orthopaedic equipment which was available in those days.
However, in the past two or three years in particular very great advances have been made in the realm of artificial limbs. If one is injured, under the workmen's compensation provisions there is in most provinces not only the opportunity for vocational training in new occupations, but there is also the opportunity of acquiring the most modern and up to date artificial aids.
If a person is not covered by workmen's compensation and has been disabled in a non-industrial accident, I should like to be assured that if he is able to assimilate vocational training he will receive assistance under this bill. Is there provision in this bill for artificial limbs to be supplied which would enable such a person to take up a new occupation? The minister nods his head, and I gather that this assistance will be forthcoming. I am certainly glad this is so, because I think it is an important part of rehabilitation.
There is also this point, Mr. Speaker. A person who has undertaken vocational training is, under the workmen's compensation provisions, in receipt of assistance which will enable him to carry on vocational training and meet his costs of living.
I presume that those who will be covered by this bill will, to perhaps a considerable extent, be drawing welfare assistance. Welfare is basically just sufficient for a bare existence, to the shame of this country. But if one is to undertake vocational training, I think I can say from past experience that a little more than straight social welfare is required.
There, also, I should like to know whether there is provision in this bill to not only take care of the actual vocational training, but also the living expenses of a disabled person while undertaking that training.
After the training is completed there arises the question of placement. The minister has made it clear that he recognizes the importance of placement and that one of the purposes of the council will be to do everything possible to see that after vocational training these disabled citizens are placed in employment. That is as it should be. Perhaps we could hear at a later stage from the minister

Vocational Rehabilitation just what emphasis will be placed on this matter and whether or not consideration will be given to some of the problems which have to be met and to the policies by which they might be overcome.
A number of industries have been doing an excellent job in the placement of disabled persons but I think it is unfortunate that to a considerable extent industry has not shown evidence of a concrete interest in this matter. I believe a major educational campaign must be waged in order to get a sympathetic acceptance by employers in this country of the value not only to themselves but to the Canadian economy and to the individuals concerned of employing a percentage of disabled persons who have received a good training. I know that in some countries in the world employment of disabled persons is governed by law. Employers who have a certain number of employees are bound to engage a percentage of disabled persons. However, I hope it will not be necessary to go to that point in Canada and that we can persuade industry to take in disabled persons from a spirit of citizenship and responsibility.
I should also like to throw out a suggestion which came to my attention recently. It is this. In some of the countries of Europe the placement of disabled persons who have been trained in certain occupations has not been left solely dependent upon possibilities of employment already in existence. The government itself takes a primary interest in the question and has established either government-owned or government-assisted concerns or small industries where only the disabled are employed. Thus there is not only a continual educational program going on to encourage private industry to take a percentage of trained disabled persons but the government itself has a direct concern in industries whose primary purpose is the employment of disabled persons. I have only been aware of this situation in recent times but I am given to understand that it has been a most successful policy and it is one which I commend for the consideration and,
I hope, the approval of the minister or of those who will have the responsibility of the administration of this measure.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, this is in our opinion a most important bill. It represents a step forward. It represents a recognition of the responsibility of government and of all those who are not physically disabled to take an interest in the rehabilitation of those who are less fortunate. We commend the government on the introduction of this bill. We shall most certainly support it and perhaps when we are engaged in the


committee stage we shall have other words to say on the details of the measure as it proceeds.

thought a member of the official opposition was about to rise. If that is the case I will resume my seat. I spoke on the resolution stage and I am going to be very brief now.
