I have a particular hobby as far as the rehabilitation of both human beings and nature is concerned. Conservation has been a hobby of mine during most of my life in these two aspects. On that account I am very pleased to see the introduction of this bill and glad to note that the expenditure for this very worth while purpose is to be on a statutory basis. Without doubt many persons who will receive training under the terms of this bill can be placed in employment as a result of that training but I am going to make reference to that smaller percentage who will find it very difficult to find employment because of certain unfortunate circumstances or the unfortunate nature of their disabilities. In some cases it is not possible to employ such people in the usual places of business or occupation. My experience in this respect and my knowledge of a number of cases throughout the years leads me to suggest we shall have to do more. Federal and provincial governments and other agencies will have to do more than simply provide for training according to the terms of this legislation. It is going to require the co-operation of all levels of government, private agencies and individuals to promote and finance, shall I say, what I consider specially organized activities in the light industrial field and in certain phases, shall I say, of light agricultural production.
As far as industry is concerned-and I have felt this for some time-we should have some method of getting together representatives of the federal government, the provincial governments, the agencies and the individuals interested to provide, say, in each constituency or suitable area some particular light industry where these unfortunate people

can be employed so as to earn their own living and have a sense of purpose in so doing. I suggest there are certain opportunities in light woodworking, the making of toys and in the making of special products from wood from waste from saw mills and other forest industries. At the present time certain industries require stocks of a certain size-small blocks of wood of a certain size; certain types of material for packaging and so on production of which could be undertaken in a light woodworking industry in which many of these unfortunate persons could be employed.
Then, as far as agriculture is concerned, I have felt there should be an opportunity for some form of state operated or co-operatively owned farm under, shall I say, state sponsorship providing opportunities for persons to engage in poultry farming and the production of vegetables and small fruits. I am speaking particularly of those persons who have to have guidance, persons who can perform simple operations and who find satisfaction in doing certain light work in association with people who care for them. In this connection I wish to bring the attention of the house to the tremendous opportunity there is in this country for the growing of black currants. That does not sound very important, but I remind hon. members that we import into Canada a very large amount of black currant jam and preserves in other forms. The demand for black currants is growing, particularly since people are becoming aware of the medicinal properties and value of black currants.
I see some hon. members smile, but there is an opportunity in this respect. We are now importing from European countries and the United States a great many of these products. I mention this as one feature of the fruitgrowing industry that could be developed under perhaps co-operative farms of the nature I indicated.
There are other opportunities which exist in this field. In the district which I represent there are thousands of acres of blueberries which go to waste every year. They are beautiful blueberries. Possibly this situation exists in other members' constituencies. There are acres of huckleberries going to waste as well. Years ago these blueberries and huckleberries were picked and shipped in carloads. Families were able to make on the average $10 a day-father, mother and child. It is almost impossible today to get people to do this sort of thing. They will pick only their own requirement and will not undertake this work in a commercial way.
Several small communities in my constituency used to ship an average of seven carloads of these blueberries to the Calgary
Vocational Rehabilitation market each year. On the present market they are worth 30 cents a pound in Calgary and other prairie points. At 16 cents per pound a person can earn a fair wage. They cost 5 cents per pound to package and transport to Calgary.
One can see the opportunity that exists here which could be developed by individuals who are interested in doing something to assist these unfortunate people. I am not suggesting this could be done overnight. It would require improved and extended legislation as well as co-operation among federal and provincial governments, private agencies and individuals. However, I do rise to make the suggestion that this is one approach to the problem faced by the more unfortunate with whom we are concerned at the present time. It is a suggestion that should be given further study in an effort to see what can be done on a co-operative basis to assist that percentage of unemployed individuals today who will never be placed in normal or usual employment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) for his remarks. He is one of those hon. members who has made me welcome in this house. I am very grateful to him in this regard.
There are certain items in the bill which the minister has proposed with which I do not agree. One of these is that the definition indicates that this legislation is to be available only to those persons who are incapable of pursuing regularly any substantially gainful occupation. The employment placement which is referred to again is such only the objective of which is to enable those persons of becoming capable of pursuing regularly any substantially gainful occupation. It is a fact that there are many individuals in this country who are disabled from disease. They may not have lost a limb, their sight or hearing but they are disabled to the extent that they are, while capable of taking training, many at their own expense, through the ordinary system of schooling in the various provinces, because of their disability-I am thinking particularly of the local individuals in my riding-unacceptable to industry. Many of these individuals have acquired clerical training and therefore do not fall within the definition of this measure because they are capable of pursuing regularly any substantially gainful employment, but nevertheless are unable to find jobs.
This is a situation which has not arisen as a result of economic conditions of the last one or two years but has existed for many

Vocational Rehabilitation years. These individuals are incapable of obtaining employment largely because of the reaction of employers and employees who are uncomfortable in the presence of these people notwithstanding the fact that they are capable of doing a job. Too many employers, and this group unhappily includes the Ontario hydro and arms of the provincial and federal governments, will not employ an individual who is disabled, although capable of doing a job and having a livelihood, because of the fact that they are in a position where they will be seen by the public, and the companies feel this is not good for public relations.
It is a most unhappy situation for those who have used their own resources to acquire training when they find they are not only unable to secure a job with private employers but on many occasions because of pension and insurance provisions-they are incapable of being insured-they are unable to find employment even with arms of the governments. I would ask the minister to consider this definition carefully, before he brings the bill before the house, as to whether it would be of benefit to widen the definition to include those individuals who are trained and capable of holding jobs but because of their appearance, resulting from an impairment, are unacceptable in employment. This problem does not involve training or re-training but is a matter of placing the individuals.
I have reference to a particular individual who has been unemployed for upwards of ten years. I employed him myself so long as I had a position open for him but before and since that time he has been to every arm of government in and out of Ontario in an effort to secure employment but has been unsuccessful because employers are afraid that his would-be fellow employees would object to his appearance.
The individuals to whom I refer should not be thrown on a garbage heap. These individuals are capable of making a contribution to our society and require the assistance of employers in placing them in positions which they are capable of handling. I would therefore ask the minister not to disregard the problems of those individuals who are trained and capable of doing jobs by excluding them under the plan of Bill No. C-84.

Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased indeed to hear the remarks of hon. members who took part in the debate on second reading of the bill in that they showed so much interest in this matter and, if I may say so, sincere interest. There is provision for prosthetic appliances as part of the restoration process and it includes limbs and all such things that are necessary. With respect to the matter of living allowance during the period of training, living allowances, proposed by the provinces and approved by the federal government are payable to these people during the period of training.
I wish to say to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that I appreciate his keen interest in this matter. He is a man of kindly heart and amiable disposition and I know that the human aspect of this matter is very close to him. The collaboration of all agencies and people is essential, of course, in this matter, including the voluntary agencies, the provinces, the federal government, the national employment service and individuals. I might say to him that the question of sheltered employment to aid in the rehabilitation of workers is receiving close study. We are always on the lookout for opportunities for the disabled in a rural setting and we have in mind such means as he mentioned. However, this is an area where more research is probably needed and we are going to do everything we can in this respect.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) referred to a particular case that had come to her attention and in which she was interested. I might say that we feel that the combination of training and counselling has a great deal to do in the placement of this type of person. In the approximately 200 national employment service offices across the country we now have some 230 special placement officers who do nothing else. They are properly trained for this work and they are engaged in counselling and endeavouring to place such people in suitable employment. They are in constant touch with possible employers and with those who are seeking employment. They are available to

these people and are more than happy to be of service to them. They too are interested in the problems of the disabled in the same way that we are, and it gives one a great glow of satisfaction to know that they have been able to help so many people who are disabled.
I have nothing further to add except to say that we hope that by having the bill passed we will be able to assure the continuation of this type of work and federal financial participation will thus be assured in the minds of the provinces.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
Clauses 1 and 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Agreement authorized.

Mr. Chairman, subclause 3 of clause 3 reads as follows:
In this section, "costs" incurred by a province means the costs incurred by the province determined as prescribed in the agreement-
I was wondering, since in a number of these cases rehabilitation might require long hospitalization, whether or not the agreement here would apply to the costs assumed by the provinces in this connection or whether the federal government assumed that they would be paying their half under the hospital insurance scheme?
Yes, we pay our half under the hospital insurance.
You would not be paying any more under this act?
Not for straight hospitalization.

In a number of these cases there is no hospital insurance. I know that happens in Ontario and the municipalities have to put up a considerable amount of money to cover the hospitalization of these people. Would the federal government be assuming any portion of that cost?
No, Mr. Chairman.
In other words, the federal government is not assuming 50 per cent of the cost of the scheme?
Yes, we are, but the hon. member is talking about something else altogether.
People who are handicapped sometimes have to be hospitalized to receive orthopaedic surgery.

This bill, Mr. Chairman, is primarily designed to take care of rehabilitation of the disabled. It is not for hospitalization. If in the particular instance the hon. member mentions, the surgery were part of 90205-6-264
Vocational Rehabilitation the rehabilitation of the person, then we would assume 50 per cent of the cost. However, if the disabled person entered a hospital because of illness and not as part of a program for rehabilitation, then that does not come within the scope of our arrangements with the provinces.

Clause 3, paragraph (1), Mr. Chairman, reads:
The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, enter into an agreement with any province, for a period not exceeding six years, to provide for the payment by Canada to the provinces-
Are these agreements with the provinces for varying periods of years as between one province and another?

Up until now the agreements have run for a period of five years. It is proposed under this bill to authorize the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces for a period of six years.

I should like to ask the minister if he knows of any of the provinces which have compensation acts under which the provinces do not supply vocational training? Are there any such provinces? I believe there are.
I am told that the provinces do not supply it, but they do have the power to pay for it.

That is the reason I was asking. I could not say with certainty, but I thought there were some provinces that did not supply vocational training to those who were entitled to benefits of workmen's compensation.
The reason this fact came to my mind was that this clause says the provisions of the bill do not apply to any disabled person whose disability is the result of any injury in respect of which benefits are payable to him under any workman's compensation law. There may be benefits which are payable because of a permanent or partial disability but there are not disability benefits. If there are compensation laws in which there are not disability benefits so far as vocational training is concerned, then this means that the people of that province, because of the dereliction of the government of that province, cannot come under this act.

Yes, the hon. member is correct, Mr. Chairman, in that respect. However, I feel it is the responsibility of the province to undertake such a program under their workmen's compensation measure. Even though the province may not have such a program we, as a federal government, would be prepared to counsel individuals in respect of this

Vocational Rehabilitation matter. 1 think the provinces should undertake such training of disabled persons, particularly under workmen's compensation acts, under which they are being trained and rehabilitated in most provinces.

Is the government assuming one half of the cost of rehabilitating persons handicapped by mental illness? The definition clause says that a disabled person means a person who, because of physical or mental impairment, is incapable of pursuing regularly any substantially gainful occupation.
I have referred before to the fact that people might be confined to hospital for prolonged periods as a result of a disability which could be corrected by orthopaedic surgery. According to clause 2 of this bill, mental impairment should apply also. I should like to know the differentiation the minister is trying to make.

Here again, Mr. Chairman, mental illness comes under provincial jurisdiction. However, if a person who has undergone treatment for mental illness is restored, then we will participate in his rehabilitation.
I should like to ask the minister if the construction of buildings and the supplying of equipment will be the subject of a 50 per cent donation from the federal government?
This bill does not take care of that. That is handled through the health grants and other means available.
As I understand it, then, the maintenance of buildings would be handled through the same branch?
Under this measure we would not participate in those costs. We are only concerned with the actual training and rehabilitation process.
The way I see the picture at the moment, then, if I may just ask another question, is that the province makes a decision as to where this work is to be performed and we accept it, in principle?
Yes.

I should like to ask the minister this rather intricate question. Here is a case of a veteran who suffers a war disability as a result of overseas service. He has a stiff leg. He is in a car accident and the rest of the passengers are able to jump out and save themselves, but because of his stiff leg this man is not able to jump out and, as a civilian, suffers a disability. Who would be responsible for retraining?

We could accept that case under this program under those circumstances.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-77, to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. Jorgenson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister this evening who, as I am sure the house knows, is away on a mission that is of importance to everyone in Canada, I take pleasure in making a few remarks on the motion for second reading of this bill to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.
At the resolution stage the minister outlined the broad philosophy which this bill is intended to convey. He stated that the main purpose is the improvement of the economic position of those farmers whose lands are at present classified as marginal or submarginal. However, it has not only the intention of improving the economic status of a great number of farmers who live in these economic units; it will also have the effect of simultaneously improving the position of farmers possessing more economic units. The bill itself fits into the broad philosophy of this government in respect of agricultural policy.
The subjects of bills that have been introduced into this House of Commons and have been passed as legislation include the following: a program of price stabilization to alleviate the effects of the fluctuation of prices owing to economic conditions beyond the farmers' control; the introduction of a crop insurance program designed to minimize the effect of fluctuation in yields caused by weather conditions beyond the farmers' control; the implementation of a comprehensive 90205-6-264J
Marginal Lands Development farm credit program to assist farmers in developing more economic units and to provide farmers with the opportunity of developing their operations to the point where they can effectively carry on in the face of changing economic conditions in the world today. This program fits into that broad general picture.
There are three attitudes that a government can take towards agriculture in the country as a whole. It could do nothing and could allow the agricultural economy to develop of its own accord. As I think most hon. members would agree, you would get the results that you should expect from that type of policy.
The second attitude is that you could leave nothing to the farmer; you could direct him completely in the production, marketing and selling of his products. We prefer not to take this attitude because we firmly believe that farmers in this country are not only capable but desirous of carrying on their own farming operations and making their own decisions on the farm.
We prefer to adopt the attitude that governments can provide an environment whereby people can take advantage of their own native abilities, initiatives and desires, and by providing that environment they can achieve for themselves that position which it is necessary for them to maintain if they are to keep pace with the other forces in our economy.
There are several approaches to this problem. The bill outlines in three separate phases the intention of the government. First of all there are the projects for the alternative uses of land.
The minister has on several occasions indicated what he has in mind in this respect. He has outlined that many areas of Canada which are presently being used for agricultural purposes could be put to better use for the production of trees or as reforestation projects.
A number of these projects have already been put into effect under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. These are designed to bring into effect the proper utilization of our land resources.
There are several other aspects of land utilization programs that I could cite. One in particular that comes to my mind at this time is the program dealing with wildlife conservation. This is a program that has often been discussed but in respect of which very little action has been taken.
It is perhaps a sad commentary on our system that in the past we have found that too often municipal programs, provincial programs and even individual programs are in conflict with national programs. I think it

Marginal Lands Development is fair to say that under the rural development program the intention will be to coordinate the efforts of not only provincial and federal governments but those of municipal and private organizations also, even down to individual farmers, in the proper utilization .and conservation of our land resources.
The definition of the word "agriculture" has often taken many meanings. The dictionary itself uses many ways of describing it. However, in my opinion the definition that most appropriately describes agriculture is not contained in the dictionary but comes from some experience and knowledge in the practical application of farming methods.
In many respects agriculture seems to be regarded by the non-farmer as a very complicated business. Perhaps this is because we are living in an age where complications are worshipped. I prefer to think of agriculture as a technique whereby you continue to produce food from the land for as long as food is needed, but you will only continue to do that if what you take out of the land is replaced.
Here again the bill does provide for proper conservation methods and, in addition to this, the development of rural projects designed to complement the existing agricultural potential of a given area.
There are many ways in which projects can be carried out under the terms of this bill. Perhaps it might be appropriate, since I am from the province of Manitoba, to outline at this point what this particular province has done in attempting to prepare themselves to co-operate with the federal government in the development of their own resources.
First of all, starting shortly after the present government assumed office, they began to conduct a land classification survey-the only one in existence in Canada-to determine the agricultural potential of each area.
Following this they have carried out several economic surveys to determine what the industrial potential, in conjunction with the agricultural potential, of a given area will be. Several of these surveys have been completed and others are currently under way.
In the economic survey areas the province has set up what they call community development corporations, composed of individuals, businessmen, bankers, farmers and whoever may be interested, to decide upon projects that might be complementary to the existing economy of that particular area.
After having decided what projects will be best suited to their particular area, these development corporations will then apply to the provincial government, through the Manitoba development fund, to assist them in carrying out the projects they have in mind.

Provided that these projects are complementary to the plans for that area, they can receive financial assistance to carry on these projects.
As I mentioned earlier, several of the projects have been completed. I should like to quote briefly from part of the report on the economic survey of south central Manitoba, by Ebasco Services Incorporated, of October, 1960. On page 75 of the report, under the heading "Guidance for Development", the third paragraph reads:
In any such plan all levels of government-
They are speaking here of plans for rural development:
-will be involved and voluntary organizations such as chambers of commerce, agricultural societies, and community development corporations must lend their assistance to a co-ordinated program.
This is a point which I made earlier, and I think it is one that is significant because it appears repeatedly throughout this report. On page 76 under the title "Land Use and Economic Planning", this is what they have to say:
Land use planning should be applied to the entire area of projected community growth of all urban centres to ensure the welfare of local citizens, the protection of commerce and industry through the prevention of improper land uses, the provision of adequate space for schools, hospitals, parks, playgrounds and industrial locations, and development of aesthetically pleasing street patterns and residential areas. It should be noted that security of investment in housing, commercial establishments and industrial plants can only be achieved if firm zoning and land use restrictions are applied consistently. At the present time new industries prefer to locate in centres with adequate land use planning. In future this preference may be expected to reach a point where location of new industries may be contingent upon such measures.
I think this indicates clearly the necessity of the implementation of this measure to assist communities and provinces in the proper utilization of their land resources. It is also interesting to note in the report of the delegation of the Canadian Department of Agriculture dated February, 1960, presented by request to the special committee of the Senate on land use in Canada, some of the observations of that body. At page 56 of the report, the following recommendations appear:
Team effort of local people.-One of the basic tenets of the rural development program is the belief that local people can do things to help themselves if they are provided with motivation, leadership and financial aid.
As I outlined earlier, this is the philosophy which this government has adopted with respect to the development of our rural areas. We do not believe we should provide complete direction. I shall read the paragraph which occurs a little later on in this report and which corroborates this attitude.

This has been accomplished through the mobilization of local citizen groups under the guidance of the federal-state extension service and many community minded leaders. It was of interest to the delegation to learn about the large number and varied kinds of projects that local leaders and committees had put into operation and were considering for future action.
Later on they say:
The fact that the members of the local committees have a personal interest in bringing about improvements in the economic and social structure of the area is the real key to success.
This underlines the point I made earlier with regard to the Manitoba program where the initiative and the direction of community development programs takes place at the local level. Once they have decided upon a course of action they can request assistance from provincial and federal governments in carrying out the program.
In the fourth paragraph it is stated:
The real problem is to stimulate imaginative and critical thinking on the part of the local people so they are able to see the potentials and opportunities and the need for action .. . This is a town-country approach, and sectional interests are lost in the common good.
Some indication of the need for focusing on local effort in the development and direction of projects was noted by the delegation in at least two different states.
This observation is very important:
Where the line of direction was from the federal or state authority down to the local level, projects failed because of lack of local interest and support. The delegation found a strong feeling that the organization and direction should remain in the hands of local people but the stimulus and motivation, especially in the early states, should come from state and federal bodies through the co-operative extension service.
I think this clearly underlines the intention of the bill which is now before the house and certainly it is an indication that in many respects we can follow the experience that our neighbours to the south have gathered in the course of their rural development programs.
Perhaps it would not be amiss if I read here tonight from a statement which appeared in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture news and information bulletin of January, 1961. It gives a fairly clear indication of what type of rural development program could be organized in an area which is in need of some reorganization. This item appears on page 2 of this bulletin and it is entitled: "A Rural Development Project in Quebec". It says:
In recent speeches, agriculture minister Hamilton has made the point that in the future many farmers would be wise to develop alternative sources of income to supplement their returns from conventional sources. He has mentioned pulp-wood as one of these alternative sources. There are no doubt others that come to mind and many have been developed in the United States under their expanding rural development program. The MacDonald Farm Journal, the monthly publication
Marginal Lands Development of MacDonald college, McGill university, edited by Leslie G. Young, the secretary of the Quebec Farmers' Association, carries a very interesting story in its December issue, which spells out how one farm family sought out an alternative source of income that has grown into a community project.
This story is set in the Sutton mountains, at the town of Sutton, 63 miles from Montreal.
I am sure the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) will be interested in this.
There are many mountains and hills in that area, and some of the farms are of a marginal type. One young farmer, Real Boulanger, a confirmed skier, decided that the community had real potential as a skiing resort. He and his family and friends organized Mount Sutton, Inc. in February of 1960, and purchased 2,300 acres of land on the north side of Mount Sutton, the highest peak within 100 miles of Montreal. Then came the development of a first-class ski resort. Experts were brought in to lay out the trails, and all summer long workers have been busy installing a double chair lift, a T-bar and building a chalet. A new road was built and parking for 2,000 cars was provided in time for the opening at mid-December. Jean Lessard, one of Canada's 1960 Olympic skiers, has agreed to provide skiing lessons. What has it meant to the community? Sutton is a rural community, and most of the local businesses were dependent upon the farm trade. The resort has brought new business. Twenty five people have been employed on the project, and it will provide full-time employment for from 15 to 20 people all winter. It is expected that the ski run will take from $60,000 to $70,000 the first winter, and that the total revenue in the community will be between $250,000 and $300,000. Real estate prices have soared, and many people have come out from the city to buy lots for country homes. The town has several new shops and stores, and there is a boom in the room and lodging business. Some 150 people in the town have listed rooms for skiers. The mayor of Sutton is most enthusiastic, and the Brome Country Farmers' Association has taken the initiative in seeking zoning bylaws to prevent the construction of substandard tourist accommodation.
This is just one example of rural development carried on through the initiative of a group of local people. It is not too difficult to imagine how many more projects somewhat similar in type could be carried on throughout Canada if some assistance in planning and financing could be given through provincial and federal governments. As I have already indicated, my own province of Manitoba is a province which is very active in laying the foundations for a development program to complement the existing economy, providing alternative uses of land, and thereby providing employment opportunities for people who are presently flocking to the cities, swelling our unemployment ranks.
It does seem to me that the intention of this bill is to create many new opportunities for farmers throughout Canada and, most important of all, to provide for the continuation of the land resources of this country so that future generations will have the opportunity

Marginal Lands Development or making their living from the soil and providing food for the nation and, indeed, for the countries of the world for as long as food is needed.
I am sure that the minister would have made a far more extensive statement at this time than I have, and I trust that when he returns he will have the opportunity of commenting further and elaborating on some of the points I have made. Knowing of his enthusiasm for the contents of this bill, and with knowledge of the energy he has applied in bringing into effect the many programs which we felt are not only desirable but necessary for the continuation of our land resources, I am sure that hon. members of this house will support this bill. I have taken a great deal of pleasure in having had the opportunity of saying a few words at this particular stage of the bill.

speechtext:
No, in one of the areas that will not need to benefit by this bill because in that area around the village of Ashern, notwithstanding the fact that the land and climate there are not as good, as in many other parts of Manitoba, there has been a great deal of skill used over the years in developing crops, particularly specialty crops, such as certain kinds of seed, as the hon. member knows, which has made that particular community-I attended last year the fiftieth anniversary of the establishment of that settlement where I went 49 years ago -one of the more prosperous areas in that part of Manitoba, although it is not favoured with the best soil and conditions such as the Portage Plains and some other favoured parts of Manitoba. I think that is a very good illustration of what can be done if there exists good community spirit as has existed in that

place throughout the whole of its history. I can speak from detailed personal knowledge because its history only began the year before I went there.
Anyone who can recall, as I can, the wave of homesteading that took place in 191011-12, and the number of people who went up there after filing at the dominion land office in Winnipeg on a quarter section never having seen the place, who spent every cent they had and ran into considerable debt, and got heaps of rocks that could never possibly be made into farms, will realize that this is not an ideal way to settle and develop a farming community. If we had had the foresight, and I am not criticizing anyone in saying this, to see what some of these problems were at that time, we would have had much less need for legislation of this kind and other legislation that has been passed over the years.
I also remember very well the period immediately after the first world war when the soldiers' settlement board was being used as a device for getting the troops out of sight as quickly as possible when the war was over. My father was in the lumber business for the short while he lived after the war and I had a good deal to do with that business at that time and, as a consequence, was in a position to realize the debts that were run up but that never were repaid because the settlers could not possibly do so. I remember the over-capitalization with respect to land that ought never to have been settled, though some of it could have been used as part of larger holdings with some advantage, in the way that it is gradually coming to be used now.
Just as in our industrial development we have developed slums because of a lack of foresight and allowing nature to take its course rather too much, so too in the rural development of Canada there is no doubt that we have something analogous in far too many parts of the country.
Then, of course, in the thirties we had the terrible disaster of the dry weather which was so ruinous to so many people who had really established themselves very well and considered that they had permanent economic security. We had to take another hard and painful look at the whole problem of use of land in the prairies of western Canada. I think that anybody who has had the privilege that I assume most hon. members have had, and which I had once again at Easter time, of driving through and flying over great areas of the southern prairies will feel that in the 25 years since the period of the great droughts we have done a great deal collectively, through the federal government and through the operations of provincial governments whatever their political character,
Marginal Lands Development to rehabilitate the prairie land so as to make more effective use of it and to provide a measure of security not against drought, because we cannot have real security against drought, but against the worst effects of drought.
I think that we in this country can take a great deal of satisfaction out of the operations of the prairie farm rehabilitation legislation in the 25 or 26 years it has been in effect. I take it that it is mainly on the experience of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration that the present legislation is based.
I am very happy to have the opportunity to recall to the minds of some hon. members who were not here at the time that the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, from the time he was counsel to the royal commission on federal-provincial relations, the so-called Rowell-Sirois commission, was very much impressed by and interested in the work that was being done on the prairies through federal soil surveys, P.F.R.A. and in other ways to conserve the soil and make the best use of it. It was largely through Mr. St. Laurent's own initiative that the ladies and gentlemen of the other place undertook the study of land use which has been drawn upon so heavily by the present Minister of Agriculture in the preparation of this legislation.
There is no doubt whatever, sir, that the extension, expansion and development of this work is an urgent problem. When all is said and done, no matter how great our industrial development, agriculture will always, at least in the foreseeable future, remain one of the main industries of this country. My own suspicion is that the economic importance of agriculture relatively, though perhaps not the proportion of our manpower engaged in it, will grow and not diminish in the next generation. I admit that is based, of course, on one very tall assumption, the assumption that we are not going to have a catastrophic world war.
But if we assume we are not it seems inevitable that the population of the world will go on growing. There is no doubt that North American agriculture is in the main so much more efficient than agriculture in any other part of the world. I am watching the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) shaking his head, but I think he will find, having regard to the number of persons engaged in North American agriculture, that production on the whole is very much greater than anywhere else in the world. It may be that in other places more intensive methods are used, but there is no place where the application of capital and of modern methods and techniques has transformed an industry more than it has transformed agriculture in
4188	HOUSE OF
Marginal Lands Development the memory of everyone in this house. When you go out to the prairies today and see the number of people required to grow much bigger crops of wheat than were ever grown in the days of the horses when the farmers had to grow fuel for the horses in the form of oats, when you see the number of people that can produce what we are producing today and realize that the only part of the world where there are great agricultural surpluses is in North America, I think that the accuracy of my general proposition would be very hard to challenge successfully.
There is another very good illustration, of course. We can produce wheat in this country and sell it in the markets of the world but unfortunately we have not yet been able to produce many fully manufactured articles that we can sell competitively in the markets of the world. In other words, generally speaking our agriculture is more efficient in world terms than our manufacturing industries are.
At the same time we have far too large a proportion of our population engaged in agriculture that is not economic in any sense of the term, in agriculture that is very close to being subsistence agriculture. I do not think we have any genuine subsistence agriculture in Canada. I do not think in a country as far north as we are it would be possible to have real subsistence agriculture, but we come very close to it in far too many areas of this country. Far too many people are devoting far too much energy to a little patch of land without having the best kind of machinery, without the best kind of methods, without the best kind of knowledge, and as a result they are getting a very meagre living.
These is no doubt that from a long term standpoint legislation of this kind, properly administered and wisely and scientifically planned, can do a very great deal of good. I think that any step forward in this direction should be applauded by every hon. member on both sides of the house. But I think there are one or two cautionary words that also ought to be said. This legislation is not going to contribute in any way at all to the solution of any of our immediate problems. Indeed, it may do the reverse unless we are very careful because, at the present time, it would be a very grave error indeed to take anyone off a subsistence farm in order to consolidate holdings and make someone else's farm more efficient and put the person removed from his farm in the slums in one of our cities on relief. That would not be an advantage. That would be a disadvantage. That would be a backward and not a forward step.


Now, I do not want to be misunderstood. I am not suggesting for one minute the government has any such intention. I do not believe it has. But I do say that we must remember you cannot consolidate these uneconomic small holdings, you cannot remove every second farm family, without having some place for these others to go. While there is a lot to be said for seeking to decentralize industry for the sake of getting small industries into rural communities where they will provide alternative occupations at certain seasons of the year, where they will provide supplementary income and so on, we ought to remember that even more urgent than getting industry into these rural areas, at any rate while the people still have farms and are still making some sort of living, is to get some industries into the coal mining areas. There are a lot of people in those areas who will not have any way of making a living at all. We have not done much of a job in that direction.
There is only one situation in which legislation of this sort can work, and that is in a dynamic, growing society. We cannot have rural rehabilitation with three quarters of a million unemployed at the same time. This is a basic fact that we have to keep in mind. It is a good thing to plan. It is a good thing to get ready so that when we do get out of the economic doldrums, when we do start on the upturn again and when there are alternative opportunities, we will be ready to take advantage of them. These are all very good things but I do hope the Minister of Agriculture who is sometimes, I believe, more blinded by his own vision than is anyone else, will not go about as the Prime Minister did on a recent television show and talk about this measure as something that is going to be the immediate economic salvation of the country. It is not. This is not to condemn it at all, but it will have no immediate effect whatever. It cannot have and, what is more, it should not have because it is going to require a lot of hard thinking and hard planning unless it is going to go on the rocks as a result of bad management or bad organization.
We have had enough of these rural schemes in our past history to be aware of the many mistakes that can be made. There has been one conspicuously successful effort at rural settlement when we did profit from previous experience, as I think everyone would agree. I refer to the administration of the Veterans' Land Act after the second world war. This required a lot of planning, a lot of careful, detailed organization in order to keep the mistakes to a minimum. I hope that in carrying out this legislation, which I am sure will meet with good will from all quarters of the

house, it will be remembered that progress forward relatively slowly will be better than one leap forward and two leaps backward. I suggest that that kind of caution is necessary in commending this legislation.
