subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In any event, I enjoyed the hon. member's speech. Indeed, I could see that he was living in the past for a short time, thinking of the pioneering days and so was I. I come from a family that was among the thousands of other families in Great Britain who were sold land at the beginning of this century for $100 to $200 per acre in British Columbia; our family was fortunate, and obtained good land. However I know dozens of people who bought rockpiles for $100 per acre, that was an obvious unplanned development. This land was sold by the department of lands headed by the father of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to various land companies in southeastern British Columbia and these land companies 90205-6-265
Marginal Lands Development sold it to green Englishmen as well as various other people from eastern Canada. We are, therefore, making some progress in respect of the utilization of land. I quite agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that we have made some mistakes and blunders in the past in settling land that never should have been settled. We have placed burdens upon people who wanted to gain their income from the soil, burdens that were completely unnecessary and in many cases unethical.
Having got those observations off my chest,
I wish to say that we support this bill which makes possible a long term program to meet a long time outstanding need, that is the rehabilitation of our rural areas on a logical, scientific basis. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, this is not going to put men to work immediately. This measure will do little, in fact, to remedy present economic circumstances. This program should have been put into effect 30, 40 or 50 years ago, but I am glad we are starting now. It will take 15, 20 or 30 years before we realize any large scale effects from its application.
The people of the United States have been considering this question, just as we have. The problem there is similar in many of the states, particularly in some of the western and southern states. Since the introduction of the resolution by the ministers, I have been looking up some of the literature that has been published in the United States and reading about some of the programs that have gone into effect. I find that in 1955 a rural development program was initiated as a co-operative effort of the federal, state and local governments, including participation by private individuals and agencies, to develop the human resources of rural America, with particular emphasis on improving the conditions of the numerous low income families, both farm and non-farm, living in rural areas. In a special message to congress on April 27, 1955, the president directed attention to the problems of low income rural families and presented a recommendation for a concerted program developed in a study and report prepared by the department of agriculture.
Then, by an executive order of the president, dated October 12, 1959, the president established a committee of economic advisers in connection with this rural development program. Since that time, there has been a great deal of interest stimulated in the various states in connection with the program to which I have referred. I have read some of the literature. I have read the programs of the various states. I have read of the cooperation between governments, federal and
4190	HOUSE OF
Marginal Lands Development state and local agencies, labour unions, farm organizations and womens' organizations. I think we could draw somewhat from their experience because they have moved fairly quickly in this direction.
However, I might say that I prefer our approach to this question by the introduction of legislation such as we are considering now which provides for the division of responsibility as outlined and for co-operation between governments as well as the funds required to give the program effect. It outlines the specific purpose of the program, provides for co-operation between governments and also the funds required to give the program effect. I prefer this. The United States program is really a program correlating the activities of the numerous agencies in the United States in a rural development program without any central piece of legislation.
However, this program is very extensive. It provides for the conservation of soil, water and wildlife, co-operatives, credit for farming, conservation and home improvement; employment assistance; extension of educational facilities in rural areas, financial aid and services necessary to rural areas; food distribution in certain poverty stricken areas; forestry and forest product development, conservation and forestry management; health and sanitation provision in small towns and in rural areas; income maintenance for old age, survivors' and disability insurance; programs for Indians; development programs in rural areas; industry development in rural areas; marketing improvement; price support; public works planning; rehabilitation of the disabled.
It is interesting to note how these programs are similar to some of ours. Then there is research and resource studies; road and highway improvement in farm areas; vocational training and the development of water resources for domestic irrigation and power purposes. That is a very large scale program to which effect is being given in various states. I was interested to note the scope of the services as outlined in this handbook which is the rural development program handbook issued by the committee for rural development program, Washington, D.C., in September of 1959.
I am particularly interested in forest conservation and forest farm management. I was interested to notice this interesting piece of literature published in connection with the development of forest industry opportunities in rural parts of the United States. I am going to quote briefly from this handbook. I was very much taken with the format and the material in this booklet. It deals with the location of saw mills and things of that type. In any event I quote from this one page in 

order to emphasize the value of a tree planning program and of tree farm management. At page 4 of this booklet it is stated as follows:
Timber owners of course benefit from the sale of timber but it is worth noting that for every dollar the timber owner gets for his stumpage an average of $17.60 more value is added to the original worth of the wood by the time it reaches the ultimate consumer. These additional dollars go out as wages for workers and income for companies engaged in harvesting, processing, fabricating, transporting, and distributing the forest product. If you don't have the industry in your community to convert your trees into forest products, those extra wood-based jobs never show up and those extra dollars just don't circulate among your people.
Then it goes on to deal with the necessity for dealing with tree planting on marginal land and the opportunities in the forest industry on a small scale and so on. It mentions particularly the possibility for the efficient and successful operation of small scale lumbering industry and manufacturing industries. It is proven from their experience under efficient management and with the co-operation of the state agencies concerned with the industries small companies can operate with eight to ten men employed producing lumber just as efficiently and just as cheaply as does a large concern under those particular circumstances.
Then I was interested to note that later on there was a reference to the fifth annual report in connection with this rural development program which interested me in view of the fact that we are now dealing with legislation to commence a similar program in Canada. I quote briefly from it. It is a very interesting report indeed. The thing that interests me is that once the leadership was given by the federal government and by the state government in co-operation with the universities farm organizations and in some cases labour organizations, co-operation was received from farmers and individuals and citizens in the smaller towns and communities to make this program work. It mentions here that there was a feeling "You have got to show me" in the first instance but as this program got rolling, its momentum increased and I am sure ours will too if we get it going. Respect and understanding developed, and respect came with understanding. I think we can learn a great deal from the five years' experience they have had in connection with this type of program. However, to quote briefly from this report:
In spite of many difficult obstacles, the rural development program has consistently been enlarged and made more effective year by year since it was announced in 1955 ...
The record of achievement and progress has been remarkable, especially with the problems to be overcome.

In 1956, less than 25 rural counties in only a handful of states had begun formal programs. Today some 210 counties in all major sections of the nation have the work underway or in the final stage.
Reports show more than 2,000 projects to improve farms, build new industries and expand existing ones, help both youth and adults to obtain the training they need, improve health, and accomplish other aims.
Thirty states and Puerto Rico now have rural development work underway. Regional meetings are going forward throughout the nation to help leaders in all states plan and inaugurate rural development activities.
The whole book is written in an optimistic tenor and gives the statistics in relation to certain developments which indicate that the optimism is justified.
Tonight we are considering second reading of this bill. It is a first and long needed step. It will require over-all and careful planning. It will require careful surveys in co-operation with the provinces of areas that are particularly going ot be attacked. Then it will require understanding on the part of the local people. When you begin to inaugurate a program of this kind you very often run into local misunderstandings or local objections. I have on occasion met men who, if you threatened to move them off 10 acres of rocky land where they had lived for a good many years would resist to the limit. There must be an understanding on the part of the local people of what the provincial and federal governments aim to do for them. I am sure that understanding and co-operation will come with the co-operation of all the government and local agencies concerned. This bill plans to improve agriculture, industrial land, water, forest and wildlife management. It is fortunate that this program has come in at this time. It should have come in years ago. However, regardless of our difficulties at the present time I believe that we are entering a period in Canadian history that presents an unusual challenge.
It is easy to do things when it is easy to do them. However, we are facing problems which will challenge our ingenuity and our ability to co-operate with one another as Canadians, whatever our status and whatever our occupation and will challenge our initiative and our wilingness to work together. I am sure that in the future-and in the very near future I may say-we are going to see more and more people turn from the large centres. As far as I am concerned, in some respects the larger cities are cesspools of iniquity. I have always been in favour of decentralization of population. Mind you, I also realize that with large cities you get great opportunities for cultural activities. Life is full of compensations. But I think people will turn more and more to the rural areas and the small towns that serve them. I see this 90205-6-265J
Marginal Lands Development coming in the future. I have found a change in young men in the last year or two. Young men coming home from the war were anxious to go into industry because of the larger wages there. These were sons of farmers. I find some of them now thinking of going back on the land.
While the income per month is less, the cash is less, a good many of them found out that at the end of the year they saved more from working on the land than they had in what appeared to be well paid jobs in the larger centres. This is because of the higher costs, the tendencies to spend more, get into debt, and so on.
I am sure that, through the rural rehabilitation program, in the rural areas there can be found all the resources required in the future, together with the necessary living and working space to enable people to live and work under satisfactory and happy conditions, with the recreational opportunities which Canadians enjoy.
Where this progam is given effect, in the years to come I am certain it will provide rural economic growth and maintain a vigorous and happy rural life.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very seldom that I take up the time of the house to discuss problems. I am particularly gratified tonight to follow the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), especially as they have both indicated their pleasure in supporting this bill.
The hon. member for Kootenay West, belonging to the very quiet and honourable group in the corner, had very little to say but to praise the bill. Like the hon. members, who preceded me in this debate I am rising to support this bill.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned several aspects of this matter, particularly those concerning the former government. He mentioned the fact that his father homesteaded. I should like to remind the hon. member that my father homesteaded also. This bill is designed particularly to rehabilitate agriculture generally, and as a son of a homesteader I look forward very much to its implementation.
I am in the particular category of farming which the hon. member mentioned. That is what is commonly known as the category of family farms. I do not think it is the intention of this government-although it may have been the intention of former governments-to remove every other farmer, as I think was mentioned, or the small family farmer.
I maintain very strongly, Mr. Speaker, and I say this for the benefit of the hon.

Marginal Lands Development member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that the family farmer in Canada today can compete quite successfully, for the very reason that he is a family farmer.
I have a farm in southern Alberta. It is a family farm. The family consists of six children, as a matter of fact. I do not wish to take up any more time of the house on this point, but I simply say this. My family and I have no trouble in producing agricultural products in competition with so-called larger and more efficient units.
This bill lends itself particularly to the conservation of soil and water. It has been mentioned this evening that it is a long term bill and we will not see any results from it in the near future. However, in supporting this bill tonight I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the subject of the conservation of soil and water. These are immediate problems, and I am quite sure there will be very rapid beneficial effects as a result of this bill.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned the community spirit being adequate in agriculture at the present time. I take rather keen exception to the fact that the community spirit should be regarded as the answer to what this government has recognized, after so many years, to be a national problem. It certainly cannot be cured any longer at the community level.
It is difficult for me to discuss this rehabilitation bill without relating it to other departments. This bill involves the question of our national economy. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), for instance, has pointed out across this country, and I think in so doing has captured the imagination of all Canadian people, what Canadian industry must do, not only to survive but to reach a proper economical level. This must apply to the agricultural economy also.
For instance, in January last in my constituency of Lethbridge, in the vegetables section of one of the chain stores I saw something that I rather disliked. I saw carrots done up in beautiful packages encased in cellophane. I picked up one of these packages and found that it came from California. Compared with the carrots that we raise in our area, these tasted like kindling wood. I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will recall what kindling wood tastes like, if he is a homesteader's son.
The point I wish to make is this. I talked to the manager of that chain store and said, "Sir, how much of this exists today in our local market?" The answer was that 80 per cent was imported. This is in an area which is supposed to be highy specialized, a highly productive area, with irrigation and years of experience; yet that situation exists.


This brings me back to my point. For the information of hon. members opposite, this is the reason I tie it in with other departments and industries in Canada, because you must complete the wheel; if you have a spoke out of a wheel, the wheel is no good.
Shortly after the war, and actually up to two or three years ago, Canada had little worry with regard to export markets, in relation to agricultural commodities. It was purely a sellers' market and producers could get almost any price for any product they wished to sell. That situation does not exist today. I could quote from Hansard, as a matter of fact, some remarks which have been made by former ministers in former governments which have actually got us nicely into some of this trouble. At that time we were promoting the sale of primary products -iron, or nickel or agricultural products, etc.-at a time when we should have been promoting secondary industry.
That brings me back to the illustration I gave a moment ago concerning the importation of agricultural products. That is actually the result of the lack of promotion of secondary industry as related to the agriculture industry. We in the agriculture industry must face the same situation as all the other industries in Canada are facing today. We must face the necessity of producing a product that will sell, and then go out and sell it, to quote the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees).
As I said previously, I am happy to follow the two previous opposition speakers who have indicated their support for this bill, because it really is something for which the country has been waiting, something of which the country has been in dire need for many years; so long, in fact, that waiting for it has almost got to be a habit. The minister who now holds the portfolio of agriculture, together with his predecessor and this government as a whole must be given a great deal of credit for initiating this bill. Certainly they had a good foundation on which to build. The foundation was the need over the years amounting to a habit that has led up to the present difficulty.
In addition to the problems of production and of secondary industry is the problem of quality control. Today in this house we talked about national design. We must also bear in mind that in addition to design we need Canadian quality. There is no one in this house I am sure who will disagree with the statement that there is no substitute for quality. Quality control goes right along with the development of secondary industry in all industries as well as the agriculture industry. In short, the rehabilitation bill which the

minister has introduced means to me as a simple farmer and as the son of a homesteader a move to restore something to its former usefulness or to its former self.
With that explanation, which is a simple explanation, I begin to wonder what the former self was and why it is not its former self today. I have discussed that at some length, pointing out some reasons for the introduction of this bill and some solutions to the difficulties of the industry itself.
Recalling the former usefulness of the agriculture industry in my area, I can go back 40 or 50 years and it brings to mind the early Mormon settlers, the pioneers of irrigation in my area. Actually, irrigation is related to commercial production in Canada. They developed this industry in our area and produced high quality products for the market in that day making use of a most abundant water supply and most fertile land. Today, markets are different. We need an even higher production. We need even more specialization if we are to compete in world markets or even in our own national market. That is why I am so happy to rise in my place in this house tonight to support this bill. My experience-and my experience has been consistent in my area for years and years because I have watched some of these things develop over the years-is that effective government action has long been needed. Actually, I have abhorred the lack of government action particularly at senior government level.
Tied in with all these things is one subject that I should like to emphasize most of all at this time, the conservation of soil and water. These older irrigation companies- and when I say older irrigation companies I am speaking of irrigation companies in my area in particular and in the constituency immediately east of me, Medicine Hat-I have seen these develop to the point where at the present time we have several irrigation companies, some 16 or 17 of them actually, which by way of comparison may be compared with a municipality since they are corporate entities.
That brings another point to mind. I see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is here tonight and I should like to recommend that corporate entities such as these irrigation companies might be considered in another year as eligibile to participate in the winter works program. These companies have reached the point today where their capital works have deteriorated to the stage where it is becoming impossible to bring them up to their former standard of usefulness.
Then again, the land, itself, has deteriorated. One irrigation company in particular has told me that they have written off 16,000 acres as being no longer useful
Marginal Lands Development land under the present set up. Now when you multiply that by at least four or five large irrigation companies that adds up to 50,000 or 60,000 acres of formerly good, prime productive soil which is no longer useful. However, it is not past redemption. To bring it back to its former usefulness would require financial aid. I think that perhaps under this bill when it is finally implemented the former usefulness of this land may be increased.
May I say with emphasis that I am happy to rise in my place tonight in support of this bill because never before in Canada's history has it been possible for the federal government to financially assist the various areas of Canada in the restoration to its former usefulness, of what I consider the most important economy in Canada, and I refer of course to the agricultural areas. This will take time but if we have patience we can succeed. There are one or two aspects of the solution which will perhaps not take as long to accomplish as some hon. members opposite think.
The problems I mentioned before in respect to drainage and spoilage in soil resulted from poor management, lack of capital for proper construction of irrigation transmission lines, and other related things, but probably the greatest fault lay in the lack of experience.
The irrigation system to which I have referred was the first applied in Canada on a commercial scale and was quite successful. However, after a period of perhaps 20 to 40 years certain practices were found to be no longer advisable. The experience gained from these unhappy times has perhaps been of value to the construction of later irrigation systems. Through this experience we look forward to increased irrigated acreage in Canada, which will lend itself to increased agricultural production.
I refer particularly to those areas of Saskatchewan which will be irrigated following the completion of the Saskatchewan dam. Surely the experience gained by the solving of the problems encountered in the construction of the early irrigated areas in Canada will be put to use in future years. The present bill will provide an answer to the irrigation problems facing many areas in this country. Although it may be said by some that additional highly specialized agricultural producing areas in our nation should not be developed, I would suggest that within a very short time the necessity of having such areas will be clear. It is essential, therefore, that we profit from the experience of past mistakes and in doing so perhaps recompense those individuals who have suffered in this regard in the past.
This bill refers to conservation of water as well as soil. In my area the conservation of
4194	HOUSE OF
Marginal Lands Development water is very important. It is perhaps more important than even we who live in that area commonly known as the dry land area, realize. I suggest we should be very cognizant of this program because the problem is perhaps more acute than most of us realize. As an example of this, I might suggest that last year there was a water shortage in the Lethbridge northern irrigation district which is primarily supplied by Old Man river which, in turn, is supplied by a rather small watershed in the eastern Rockies, and particularly the Livingstone gap.
Some of the younger people in that irrigation area consider there was a water shortage last year and that the lack of supply was abnormal. However, the long term record shows that it was actually a normal year. I would point out that some of the older hon. members, including perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and myself, will remember the drought years. If one could picture conditions following perhaps one, two, three, four or five drought years in relation to last year's normal condition one could realize what might happen if water is not without adequate storage, it is not difficult to visualize the effect on water supply of a drought period followed by, let us say, a forest fire, in the relatively small area of the eastern Rocky mountain watershed. I would suggest these facts have contributed to the present shortage, not only in our area but also downstream.
Mr. Speaker, I must apologize for dealing with the problems of other government departments, and in this case I refer to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and the Department of Forestry, but I would strongly urge that immediate surveys be made for the location and development of extra water storage facilities, and a program developed to prevent the over-grazing of forest reserves. I make these suggestions not only in respect of my own area but in respect of areas to be developed in the future, such as these areas in Saskatchewan to which I have referred.
Mr. Speaker, to digress for a moment, I would like to commend the ministers of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Labour for introducing the vocational training bill. This has established a precedent. Never before in Canadian history has it been possible by way of legislation for the federal government to contribute financially to such a vocational training scheme. This again must be related to agriculture because, as I pointed out a moment ago, there was a lack of knowledge which resulted in what some people might call poor management. In this day and age in a highly competitive economy, it is all the more necessary that there be specialized


training in this particular sphere of the Canadian economy. I am sure that a vocational training scheme properly utilized can be applied usefully and certainly can be a great benefit to this rehabilitation program.
With the permission of the house I should like to dwell for a moment on vocational training, what I term real vocational training compared with what has been the practice of the departments of education in the various provinces of our nation. Possibly I am going a little far afield but my experience has been that in Alberta, for instance, our young people of high school age spend two, three or four years taking a course in agriculture, mechanics, welding or farm management and after they have spent that period of time in study they are not given any certificate. So far as education in Canada today is concerned, I think we are hampered and held back by hidebound provincialism when, from the national point of view and having in mind the state of transportation and communications today, our education should be on the basis that we are a member of the world community. I hope that as the provinces take advantage of the vocational training scheme, and I am relating it at the moment to agriculture, the provincial departments of education will see to it that after our young people have spent two, three or four years at high school they will not only receive a certificate when they graduate but will have received what I would describe as true vocational training.
By that I mean simply this. The student spends his time on automobile mechanics, a business course or an agricultural course and at the same time there should be a well-rounded program including such subjects as commercial law, business English and so on so that when the young person graduates with a certificate he will have a well-rounded education and what I regard as a real vocational or technical training.
Probably I should apologise for taking so much of the time of the house in mentioning other departments but all this must tie in because it is purely and simply related to this problem. I should like to emphasize that the agricultural industry is no different from any other Canadian industry. It must meet competition. When I was home during the Christmas recess and again at the Easter recess I was sorry to see all the imported products. I do not blame Canadian industry as a whole. It is true that Canadian industries must do their part. Government legislation cannot do everything. As we have been told many times, it is hard to help people who will not help themselves. However, I have great faith in the people who contribute to the agricultural economy of Canada. In my estimation this bill

makes it possible for the first time in Canadian history for them to go ahead on their own and certain financial assistance is provided that is available for the first time in Canadian history.
I should like to urge the departments concerned to have in mind soil and water conservation and the restoration of these assets for the benefit of the agricultural industry of Canada, particularly so far as my area is concerned which should be an area of specialized production of a product of good quality that is readily marketable not only in Canada but in the export markets of the world.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to express certain opinions relating to the general principles found in the bill. Having regard to what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), in order to ensure that members will listen to what I have to say I feel I should establish my connection with agriculture.
I am pleased to say that I was born and raised on a farm in the Verner region of northern Ontario which is known to be one of the most active agricultural areas in that part of Ontario. The hon. member who preceded me as well as other hon. members expressed surprise that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) should be the first speaker on behalf of the Liberal party this evening in regard to this matter. It is my conviction that any member of the opposition who at one time held a ministerial post is definitely of the required calibre and fully qualified to speak on most problems that are of such interest as the bill we are now discussing, and undoubtedly the Canadian people realize that.
I also regret very much that while we are discussing the fundamental principles of this bill having to do with agriculture a measure which the government undoubtedly considers should receive the greatest of attention, the standing committee on agriculture, directed by the house to study the problems of that industry, is at present sitting and has sat all day.
I did not attend the meeting of that committee tonight, but chose to speak on this matter. I think it is most unfortunate, and the finger is pointing at those who engineer the business of this house, that this evening we find many hon. members who have made special studies in connection with this matter unable to attend to listen to the remarks of other hon. members or make contributions themselves. They should be entitled to do so.
There are principles in this bill, Mr. Speaker, with which I do not necessarily fully agree. There is one in particular upon
Marginal Lands Development which I should like to touch. This bill mentions the possibility of further research into agricultural problems. Undoubtedly this is a field from which the people engaged in agriculture can receive the most benefit. The government should make sure these people receive the best technical assistance and the best advice as to production methods.
On the other hand, if you read through the entire bill in an attempt to find the major principle, and if you leave aside the desire for greater research into agricultural problems, you find the bill then becomes a mere political pamphlet. In this bill there is a preamble such as we do not find in other bills of this nature. We find, too, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) is given powers by means of which he may become involved in the problems of other departments. If one reads the bill one can readily see how the Minister of Agriculture may become involved in the problem of unemployment. The minister also has unlimited authority to become involved in major river projects. Anyone reading the bill will realize that the South Saskatchewan river project could have been initiated by the minister on his own authority. Furthermore, the bill contains no provision as to the amount of money which may be involved in any agreement that may be made with the provinces.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that according to the British North America Act agriculture is partly the responsibility of the federal government and partly the responsibility of the provinces. The phraseology which is employed in this bill leads one to believe that the Minister of Agriculture could pay 100 per cent of the cost of a project within a province. In my opinion we do not find this type of provision in other bills which we have discussed here on previous occasions. The usual practice has been to state the extent to which the federal government could become involved under the bill. The powers given to the minister by this bill are absolutely unlimited. Although the farmers do receive some encouragement from this measure with regard to the research that would be undertaken, I feel it would be most dangerous to accept all the principles which are set forth in the bill.
I shall be most pleased to bring to the attention of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Jorgenson) certain clauses of the bill which give the minister unlimited power when the measure is discussed in committee. I shall refer also to those provisions which enable the minister to take over responsibilities of other departments.
I am certainly in support of what I consider to be the main principle of this bill, namely

Marginal Lands Development ways and means for encouraging further research into the problems of agriculture. Undoubtedly, the farmers cannot do this for themselves because they lack the equipment, the laboratories and so on to do this work. Agriculture is one of the most important industries in Canada, and at this time the government should certainly promote the necessary research to assist the farm population in taking care of their soil, finding better methods of controlling the soil as well as ways and means of conserving water. We fully realize that the implementation of this bill will assist our farmers, and for that reason we are in favour of it. Certainly when we are discussing the measure in committee, Mr. Speaker, I shall indicate the points which I consider to be wrong in principle.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly very glad to be able to speak in support of Bill No. C-77. Those of us who come from the province of Saskatchewan and who have watched the career of our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for many years, are proud to be able to speak in support of a bill which will endeavour to divert submarginal and marginal farms to more profitable use. This evening we have heard some discussion which has been broad in its aspects but rather vague in some of its generalities. I have listened to some of the opposition members speak, and particularly the last hon. member who referred to the principles which are involved in this bill.
Those of us who have been closely associated with rehabilitation in the past do not have to go very far to find on what principles this bill is based. Twenty six years have now elapsed since the inception of the prairie farm rehabilitation program in 1935 under a Conservative government, to deal with the immediate problems of drought and soil drifting which were then having severe effects on agriculture in the Canadian prairies. During this period of time many policies and projects have been undertaken, varying widely in their nature and scope, to meet the various situations.
Basically, however, they have all had as their one objective better land utilization and more efficient use of available water resources as a means of providing greater security and stability for prairie agriculture. I do not want to apologize at the moment for bringing in prairie agriculture, Mr. Speaker, because we will find in the application of this bill, principles which are fundamental to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, an act which provided for the rehabilitation of agricultural land and the development of rural areas.

In this connection, much progress has been made and much valuable knowledge and experience has been gained on which to base future long range land and water conservation planning in western Canada. Initially, this work has involved the introduction of those systems of farming, land use, and water supply, which would provide greater economic security for the agricultural population on the prairies and more recently, the development of larger and more comprehensive land utilization and water development schemes that will serve entire agricultural districts and prairie communities.
Cultural improvements which have been made have led to almost a completely new approach to the economics and practice of dry land farming. Techniques in soil management and methods of making more efficient use of limited supplies of soil moisture available, have been developed and are now in common use, which have helped materially to minimize the drought problem in drier area. The development of assured farm water supplies throughout the drought region for domestic, stockwatering and irrigation purposes, has also contributed greatly in bringing about more stable agriculture over a wide area. In particular, the development of assured feed supplies through irrigation for the winter feeding of livestock, and the provision of reserves of feed to carry livestock over periodic dry periods, has given much increased stability to the livestock industry and has been a major factor in encouraging greater agricultural diversification in the plains region.
Finally, the permanent removal from cultivation of lands which have proven submarginal for cereal crop production, and the fencing, regrassing, and other improvement of such areas for community pasture purposes as well as the resettlement and rehabilitation of farmers operating such lands, principally to irrigation projects, has been a major factor in bringing about necessary adjustments in the pattern of land use required on the prairies.
Where these adjustments have been of considerable benefit to the agricultural economy, new and growing demands for water required by larger municipal and urban centres for domestic and industrial purposes, as well as to support large-scale irrigation, have made necessary the development of larger and more comprehensive water storage and irrigation schemes where more dependable and plentiful water supplies can be obtained. To this end, P.F.R.A. in more recent years, has devoted an increasing amount of its attention to this type of development.
Under the terms of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, an initial appropriation of

$4,750,000 was made to cover the cost of rehabilitation activities for a period of five years, and an advisory committee was established by the act to give leadership to the program.
Rather than establish new services, existing agricultural services were given assistance to expand their operations to handle the work. In particular the experimental farms service played a major role. As the P.F.R.A. program developed, however, a separate administration vas set up in Regina in 1936 to direct water development, while the cultural improvement program continued under the direction of the experimental farms service. Then by amendment to the act in 1937, the P.F.R.A. was extended to include land utilization and resettlement.
It was realized, however, that for the development of a sound agricultural economy on the prairies, more long term measures for rehabilitation would be necessary. In 1939, therefore, additional financial allocations were made and the five-year limitation to the P.F.R.A. was removed.
From the way in which P.F.R.A. has developed, it can be seen that it certainly gave us a sound basis for expansion in the act we have before us tonight. There are other aspects of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which I am sure will be of interest to those who come from those areas where they can be applied. I want particularly to deal for a few moments with land utilization and resettlement. In order to provide for this type of program an amendment was made to the P.F.R. Act in 1937. The act was broadened in its scope to include land utilization and land settlement. This opened the way for a program which has had a far-reaching effect on the stability of agricultural production in many areas throughout western Canada. By agreement with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, lands not considered suitable for cereal crop production may be transferred to the federal government for development by P.F.R.A. into community pastures.
The province concerned selects the area to be developed and obtains control of the land. The land is then leased to the government of Canada which in turn agrees to construct, maintain and improve community pasture facilities in the area selected. In this way land subject to the hazards of soil drifting is removed permanently from cultivation and is again protected by a grass cover.
As these submarginal and marginal lands are converted into productive pastures, livestock production on the surrounding farms is being increased, thus making possible a greater diversity of farm income. Since the community pasture program began in 1937, a
Marginal Lands Development total of 1,886,364 acres of land have been developed into 65 separate pasture units. These pastures, primarily intended for reserve grazing areas to supplement farm and ranch pastures, are now providing controlled spring, summer, and fall grazing for over 120,000 head of stock annually belonging to some 6,331 farmers. In addition, a considerable tonnage of hay and some grass seed has frequently been harvested from these pastures. The program of pasture improvement carried on by P.F.R.A. has provided leadership to farmers in the development of their own farm pastures.
The resettlement of farmers from these submarginal areas has been handled jointly by the federal government and provincial governments concerned. Where available, the provincial governments provide suitable crown land on which to resettle farmers. P.F.R.A. in turn accepts responsibility for moving the farmers and their effects to their new locations, and the development of the submarginal areas turned over to P.F.R.A. for pasture purposes. Every effort is made to resettle farmers on lands which are located close to existing or proposed pastures so that the farmers may take advantage of the supplementary grazing facilities the pastures provide.
Where it has not been possible to find crown lands suitable for resettlement, P.F.R.A. has provided its own through irrigation development. Two such schemes have been built specifically for resettlement purposes in Alberta. The first involved the development of a large block of land adjacent to the eastern irrigation district called the Rolling Hills project, on which 118 farm families from the drought areas have been moved. The other is the Bow river irrigation project where approximately 27,000 acres in an area called the Hays district has been set aside for resettlement. There are now 162 farm families settled in the district.
Similarly on somewhat the same principle, five resettlement and rehabilitation projects have been built in the heart of the drought area in southwestern Saskatchewan. The only difference is that for these projects the purposes and objectives of the resettlement and rehabilitation program have been achieved without necessarily involving the movement of farmers to new locations. The five schemes, namely the Valmarie, Eastend, Consul, Maple Creek and Swift Current irrigation projects, are subdivided into 40-80 acre plots which are leased out or sold to farmers in surrounding districts for feed production. On the irrigated land, farmers can be assured of producing adequate and

Marginal Lands Development dependable winter feed supplies as well as reserves of feed to carry stock over prolonged drought periods.
In a similar manner hundreds of farmers have been rehabilitated without the necessity of moving from their farms by the development of farm-size and small community irrigation schemes built throughout the prairies with P.F.R.A. assistance.
With regard to water development, this work is carried out under the supervision of the water development division of the agricultural services branch. Projects constructed under this program are divided into two main categories according to the size of the project, the number of people benefiting, and the cost of construction. These include individual and neighbour projects, and community projects.
Individual and neighbour projects include those works which serve the needs of one or two farmers. These are generally in the form of small dams and dug-outs that supply water for stockwatering and domestic use, and/or for irrigation purposes. In such cases P.F.R.A. provides all engineering services required to plan and design the project, and a portion of the construction costs.
The rate of assistance paid on individual projects is based on yardage of earth moved and amounts to seven cents per cubic yard up to a maximum of $250 in the case of dug-outs, $300 for stockwatering dams and $600 for irrigation projects.
Where two or more farmers pool their water resources to build neighbourhood projects, assistance is paid up to a maximum of $1,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that when I began discussing this bill I said it was based on rehabilitation. The principles of rehabilitation have been well advanced under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the principle of which will be the basis of the present legislation.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act will be taken over by this bill in so far as concerns the rehabilitation of agricultural land and the development of rural areas, and will be an integral part of that act. For this reason I believe it is most relevant to show hon. members what they can expect under the advancement of this legislation.
I have not very much more to say, Mr. Speaker. However, I should like to mention that while the immediate needs of farmers are being met by P.F.R.A., attention has also been given in more recent years to the construction of larger irrigation and reclamation projects involving the development of many thousands of acres of land.
Such undertaking are in line with the long range land use plan to provide for expansion and stability in Canada's growing economy. Of 'an estimated 3 million acres of potentially irrigable land in western Canada, 1| million acres have been or are in the process of being developed. The aim is, when conditions warrant, to develop the remainder of this valuable resource.
The development of these large irrigation and reclamation works in western Canada, which either because of their size or location have not been included under the regular P.F.R.A. appropriation, has in recent years been under the supervision of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration.
These projects are undertaken by agreement between the federal government and the provincial government concerned, on a cost sharing basis. Special authorization of parliament is of course required for the construction of these major projects.
In conclusion, may I remind the house that this will of course be a fairly expensive project. However, the money will be used to make productive what is not now productive, or is only scantily so. It will be used to train farmers in different and more productive types of farming. It will be used to preserve the remaining natural resources of this nation, which we hope can be restored to their natural value.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in my place tonight with the sincere desire, in speaking on this measure, to bring to the attention of hon. members of this house the absolute necessity at this time

of acting on this measure which deals with the conservation of soil and water resources, and the terrible consequences of any delay on the part of the governments concerned.
I confess that I am indeed greatly disturbed by the tenor of the opinions expressed by the hon. members in opposition tonight and in other discourse on this measure. These hon. members seem to be dealing in generalities and political expediency rather than with the consequences of such a measure in relation to agricultural and other resources of this great nation of ours.
I am sure that if they indeed understood the ramifications of this bill they would be more fully aware of the absolute necessity that we act, and at the earliest opportunity.
The quotation commonly used, that familiarity breeds contempt, can in no manner be more fully illustrated than in regard to the attitude of some of the occupants of this country toward its soil. Soil is a commodity of which it was thought that we, a comparatively new country, had an endless supply. The degree of fertility of soil is the very basis of the life of humans on this earth today.
This soil is not unlimited either, because it is only the very top few inches of soil which is the direct source of the world's food supply for man and beast.
I think the contempt with which we treat this vital resource is truly appalling. Consider even the descriptive names that we use, such as earth, dirt, filth, mud, dust and grit. These are hardly terms of endearment. Indeed, our disregard for this commodity in this country has reached such a degree that it is a fact that we have in Canada more fertile soil covered by broken down machinery and used cars than the total fertile soil area that can be found in some countries.
In this country we take soil, and what do we do with it? We dump it in rivers; we put it in swamps; we use it to fill lakes, crevices, craters and ravines. We seem to do everything that we can to be rid of it.
On the other hand, in other countries it may be looked upon almost as a treasure. If found, it is carried home gently in a pail, a cloth or even a basket and is carefully tended in order to produce a tiny quantity of food for a hungry people.
It is well known that in regard to food prouction per given unit of soil, our country either equals or excels any other nation in the world. It is true that our basic agricultural problems today are perhaps caused by the overproduction of various kinds of food. Why would an area such as Kent county, which I represent-or indeed all southwestern Ontario, which is one of the high production areas of food in Canada-
Marginal Lands Development have need of a conservation program for soil and water? What need have we for tree farms, community pastures, or indeed government aid under a bill such as we have before us tonight?
I should like to elaborate on this point because I fear hon. members are not aware that we in these areas of high production have perhaps some of the most submarginal land that can be found in Canada today. May I point out to hon. members that too often when disaster is about to strike the indications are least evident. This is a fact often borne out by history. Hon. members will recall the history of the races of Indians who used to inhabit Central America and the southern United States, nations which were in an advanced state of civilization. Their main food was corn. This corn was grown on ground from which the virgin forest had been burnt off. This burning served to kill the weeds and sterilize the ground. It provided a fertile source for the corn, and the process served very well for two or three years. When the time came when the weeds had choked out the corn it was a common practice to burn off another part of the forest and move to the new area.
These nations practised no form of conservation and their neglect led to terrible consequences. Indeed, when there was no more virgin forest left to cultivate the nation almost starved to death, because when the weeds choked out the corn they had no method of controlling them, not even that of pulling out the weeds.
We can recall the dust bowls in the United States, in our own west and in other countries, dust bowls caused by the scarcity of rainfall and by our own agricultural practices which remove the grass cover. May I dare to say that lack of knowledge and direction is more serious than most people imagine or could even dream? As I pointed out, lack of proper conservation even in our richest farm land is causing us to lose our topsoil fertility at the rate of hundreds of thousands of tons, not in a generation but each and every year. Farmers are the first to become aware of the forces that are constantly at work to waste and destroy this greatest of our national resources, fertile soil, which is in effect the lifeblood of our world.
All too often the picture conjured up by the word "erosion" is the rushing of water caused by melting snow or heavy rains pouring down the hills and slopes to creeks and rivers and carrying with it topsoil from the surface in its violent rush and depositing this soil in lakes, rivers and oceans. This is witnessed today by the tremendous expenditure each year on dredging this sediment from

Marginal Lands Development channels and river mouths. This erosion is a fact, but I might point out that it represents only a small part of the picture. There are other ways in which soil is eroded, not so violent but equally deadly, and these processes are at work on our soil 24 hours of every day.
One of them is our method of farming. By constantly cropping for cash crops we remove tons of essential elements from the soil and return little in their place. The cultivating methods used by farmers today tend to keep our soil in a loose, friable condition in which it is most liable not only to erosion by water but to seeping down in fine particles through the soil itself into the subsoil out of reach of the searching roots of plant life where, very often, through man-made underground water drains they are ultimately carried by surface water to rivers, lakes and seas.
May I have the indulgence of the house to illustrate by a small example the magnitude of the problem? In an experiment conducted by the soil and water conservation research centre, Ohio, as reported in the February 1961 issue of "Successful Farming" on page 47, the following facts were noted as having been achieved. Each of two watersheds was planted to corn following two years of meadow. Here is the manner in which the two identical watersheds were treated in order to determine the amount of possible erosion and the effects, if any, of a planned conservation program which took the form of a change in the accepted practice in the planting of a crop of corn. The one was ploughed across the slope, disked twice, harrowed once, planted on the contour, and cultivated twice to control weeds. Hon. members familiar with this crop will, I am sure, agree this is normal procedure. The fertility level of this tract was low; the soil was limed to a PH of 5.4-this is an index reading of the degree of acidity of the soil-and an alsike red clover-timothy mixture was the meadow crop ploughed under.
The conservation method, one of minimum tillage, was ploughed on the contour, following the natural curvature of the slope, throwing the furrow slices uphill. The planting operation followed the ploughing, planting inside the tractor wheel tracks, and there was no further working of the soil, hence the term minimum tillage. This watershed had a high level of fertility; it was limed to a PH of 6.8 on a ploughdown of clover-alfalfa-timothy mixture. The run-off and eroded soil were measured on each watershed and the results seem almost unbelievable. In one season, the results of the conventional method as compared to the conservation method were as follows based on a unit of one acre; water run-off, 98,000


gallons compared to 270 gallons; top fertile soil 7.1 tons compared to 60 lbs; yield, 70 bushels of corn compared to 82 bushels. What better proof is needed of the tremendous need of a conservation program in our best farming areas?
How can we detect erosion? Does it require a trained technical expert and elaborate experimental equipment? Not at all. Anyone who takes the trouble to really see the soil they look at, can see it all around them. First, there is often a very marked decrease in the amount of produce derived from a given area of land. The character of the soil itself often changes very radically and instead of being soft, granular, sweet-smelling and springy, it becomes hard, cement-like in texture, resistant to water penetration and has a tendency to dry very quickly and blow very easily.
To this, however, is added the more insidious and dangerous fact that the food from such soil becomes constantly lower in its nutrient content. There is less mineral content, less protein, carbohydrates, and in some instances a tremendous scarcity of the trace of essential elements normally found in such foods, with the result that such food used for man or beast can cause many diseases and malformation directly attributable to malnutrition. For further proof we have only to compare the chemical analysis of such food with those produced from new or virgin soil. The difference is startling in its magnitude.
We find also that not only are crops on eroded soils stunted and of lower food value, but are more adversely affected by the elements and by drought, and far more subject to attack by disease and insects with a consequent further drop in production. It is true we have learned to augment some of the fertility of the soil by chemicals called fertilizers but even to these we have to continually add more and more elements to spur production. In many instances even this fails and the farmer soon learns that fertilization is a medicine and not a cure.
One other effect of soil erosion is the reduction of soil population. Hon. members know, I am sure, that soil should be living. Every cubic inch of soil contains billions of micro-organisms so very necessary for the growth of plants and the production of food. These micro-organisms work on insoluble elements in the soil and, either by the production of acids or enzymes, or concerted action with other species, reduce rocks, elements and vegetable matter to a substance, soluble and in a form available to plants as a food. When these micro-organisms are not in the soil in sufficient numbers, plants will not thrive or even grow at all.

Farmers can see this on their farms. Vegetation ploughed down in the fall should be worked on by these organisms and by the next growing season should be broken down to a rich black mulch containing a high percentage of plant food. In a great many instances today, ploughs are turning up vegetation of a previous year almost in identical condition as ploughed down. The microorganisms are not there and the soil becomes hard in nature, difficult to work and water runs off instead of percolating through. As a result we have a poor farm incapable of providing a normal standard of living for the occupants. This complete breakdown in soil is the direct result of erosion aided and abetted by the elements and could, if allowed to proceed unchecked, starve a nation.
Fortunately through the years by trial and error, by research and experiment, man has learned to combat this force to a limited degree; limited only by finance which curtails the necessary experimental work, and by legislation which would provide a coordinated and directed effort to fight this erosion-in other words, soil conservation. For this reason I wish not only to go on record as strongly supporting the principle of this bill, but to ally myself with the hon. members for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Campbell) and Halton (Mr. Best), and other hon. members who have long advocated a federal agriculture research committee to co-ordinate all experimental work in agriculture in order that advances may be much greater with far less duplication. These hon. members are on record as being in support of this proposal and I too wish to be placed in that category.
May I now pay tribute to industry which has recognized this problem to a remarkable degree. In Kent county very many industries, such as fertilizer companies, canning companies, and some machine companies, as a public service will either themselves test a farmer's soil for deficiency and recommend fertilizer and tillage methods to correct these defects, or using a local company, such as the C & D Sugar Company, who run experimental farms in the area, carry on research, grow demonstration crops and hold field days to enable the farmers to observe the results for themselves, and all of this at no cost to the farmer, except an earnest desire on their part to conserve and preserve the fertile soil to increase its productivity. This company-and as I am proud to say many companies in Kent county; Libby's Canners, C.I.L. and Canada Packers-actually has a staff of agricultural specialists available at no cost to farmers to aid and advise in all matters of soil conservation and production.
Business of the House
At this time I would like to pay tribute to the agricultural schools, colleges and agricultural representatives who have graduated from these schools and colleges, who offer such tremendous help in pointing out the value of soil conservation, and who have introduced practices to combat the deadly scourge of erosion.
May I suggest to hon. members that the problem of soil and water conservation of this nation should not be left entirely on the shoulders of such companies, noble as is their effort, but should instead be guided and co-ordinated by a joint federal-provincial agency. This agency should have the end in view of accomplishing the maximum amount of conservation in the minimum amount of time, and have sufficient funds placed at their disposal to allow them to begin the great measures necessary to counteract the tremendous forces of erosion ever present in Canada today.
I fail to see why all hon. members cannot endorse this measure completely. I would like to go on record as supporting this bill in its entirety and would very seriously entreat all hon. members to look into this aspect of soil erosion of our very fine farm lands today.
